sections.title: Woord Vooraf In Memoriam (p.2)
sections.text: FOREWORD In your hands, you have the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2017. In this report, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, as well as the actions taken by the shore organization to facilitate these deployments. The Navy made a significant impression during SAIL and the Marine Days in Den Helder. Old sailing ships and new war vessels were simultaneously on display in and around the Nieuwe Haven. Additionally, marines landed with heavy equipment onshore for the interested public. With thousands of visitors, it was a great success and a wonderful opportunity to showcase what the Navy has to offer. Prominently featured in 2017 was emergency aid. After the devastating hurricane Irma, Sint Maarten was particularly in ruins and there were significant shortages of basic necessities. Various ships set course for the affected island to provide assistance and deliver supplies. Marines were also deployed to ensure that the aid could be distributed safely among the population. The personnel underwent many new training courses and participated in (international) exercises. At the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the navy was present with marines and ships to introduce visitors to the naval forces. We hope that this Yearbook will prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Yearbooks Royal Netherlands Navy. Foreword On September 22, Lieutenant General (ltgenmarns) R. Verkerk handed over command of the Naval Forces to Vice Admiral (vadm) R.A. Kramer.

sections.title: Organisatieoverzichten (p.7)
sections.text: 3_Navy_Annual_Report_2017_ORGANIZATION_OVERVIEWS-7 18 Organization Overviews Department of Finance and Control (F&C) Head: Captain (ktz) M.F.C.M. Spierings The F&C department carried out its tasks consisting of supporting the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) by providing for the preparation, execution, progress, and quality of financial policy advice. Additionally, it included the composition of the budget and the establishment of the spending program, the execution of financial management as well as contributing to information provision. This was done through management and steering reports and by preparing the cash forecast quarterly, which also included proposed measures to remain within the financial frameworks. The expenditures by CZSK (Article 2 of the defense budget) were higher than expected. This increase was largely caused by additional expenses for maintenance and higher salary costs due to the agreed labor conditions agreement. With the establishment of the coalition agreement, there is a turning point after years of cutbacks and a rising budget. At the beginning of 2017, however, savings measures were still necessary, such as reducing the number of sailing days by replacing the ship in the West not in the Caribbean but in the Netherlands and accepting a short absence in the operational area during transit. Throughout the year, financial space re-emerged, which the Navy has used among other things to

sections.title: Organisatieoverzichten (p.8)
sections.text: Organizational overviews were used to purchase additional spare parts and to increase the stocks that had diminished in recent years in order to improve material readiness. With the coalition agreement, it was also decided to incorporate the budget of the Coast Guard in the Caribbean into the Defense budget, and CZSK (Royal Netherlands Navy Command) processed these adjustments in the administration throughout the year. To improve cost insight, various studies were conducted. As part of the 'Replacement of the Walrus Class' project, a cost-benefit analysis was carried out, and interdepartmental cooperation was involved in completing a policy study on the costs of readiness. One of the recommendations was to develop a cost-to-readiness model. CZSK contributed to this by developing a standards system to better substantiate the budget in terms of activities and products. A standardized approach is increasingly being used in the Policy, Planning, and Budget Cycle. In terms of personnel, this is done with averages and standards for other personnel expenditures, and for weapon systems, defense-wide established standardization sheets are used. Finally, F&C (Finance and Control) conducted many analyses for the growth plans in the context of the Development of Armed Forces (DOKM). Many types of ships will be replaced in the coming years, which requires further analyses of the expected future operating costs. The department is also taking many measures, for example, in the context of the safety organization, with personnel expansions and intensifications of activities, resulting in higher expenditures. sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.2)
sections.text: Directorate of Personnel and Operations The Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DPBV) is the supporting directorate within the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) and the Coast Guard in the areas of personnel, training, healthcare, organization, operations, and information provision. Additionally, the directorate serves as an important link to the Defense Staff/Administrative Staff through the Integration department. For 2017, the focal points of the directorate were: Optimizing operations in the broadest sense of the word. An important step was taken with the establishment of a new business plan, which will be further developed in the coming years. Personnel from Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman working on the bridge. Simplified organizational chart of the Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DPBV).

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.3)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-3 22 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Ensure that the personnel establishment of CZSK is fully filled in 2020, with a target of 98% in permanent positions and 2% flexible deployment consisting of reservists and hired personnel. To achieve this, the P-continuity project started in 2015, aimed at further professionalizing personnel management and care within CZSK. This involved matters such as Professionally Oriented Training (BGO), employability, leadership development, and ensuring integrated healthcare. Intensifying collaboration between (internal) Defense, civil regional (in training), and international partners. Intensifying the management role of CZSK for the Coast Guard Netherlands and CARIB, with special attention to long-term sustainability. Further developing the adaptability of the CZSK organization to changing circumstances, both within Defense and in society. This particularly applied to the supporting and administrative processes. In practice, this proved to be considerably more challenging, but the organization must be sufficiently prepared for the future, and therefore it is deemed necessary for this process to continue. The minehunters Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen (left) and Zr.Ms. Schiedam (right).

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.4)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-4 23 Directorate Personnel and Operations Legal Affairs (JUZA) Head: Captain (ktz) mr. G. Souer The JUZA department is part of the DP&O, one of the five line directorates of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). The department advises and supports CZSK, the directors of CZSK, and commanders of units on all legal issues that arise. JUZA provides legal advice and acts as a point of contact for the directors and commanders within CZSK. Additionally, JUZA monitors the legal and administrative diligence of operations within CZSK. The main areas of law that the department deals with include (military) criminal and disciplinary law, operational law, and state and administrative law. These areas of law are organized into three different bureaus. Thus, every employee at JUZA can function as a first point of contact (counter function) for questions directed to the department. JUZA does not provide legal advice to individual military personnel, but does assist them if necessary. In criminal or disciplinary matters, JUZA is primarily involved on the side of CZSK and the Ministry of Defence as an organization. Should a military member be involved in a criminal case, they can receive assistance from the Ministry of Defence in this matter. Personnel and Organization (P&O) In 2017, several important steps were taken within the Ministry of Defence that also had an impact on the Personnel and Organization (P&O) domain. It was decided to make the organization more adaptive, a start was made with DOKM, and in November an agreement was reached on a collective labor agreement for 2017-2018. As part of the Adaptive Armed Forces, the Bureau Flexible Capacity was established within P&O. This bureau originated from the Bureau Reservists. The latter agency was engaged until June in the deployment and administrative support of the reservists of the Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve. In addition to continuing this task, the Bureau Flexible Capacity was established as the coordinator for external hiring and deployment of temporarily available military and civilian personnel. In 2017, CZSK began with DOKM. A project organization was set up for this purpose. DOKM for CZSK involves: the expansion of operational (combat) support. In the coming years, these expansions will be implemented, which will lead to an increase in mine countermeasure capacity, the establishment of a Fleet Marine Squadron, and the construction of a Combat Support Ship.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.5)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-5 24 Directorate of Personnel and Operations After a long negotiation process, an agreement was reached at the end of November between the Defense leadership and the trade unions regarding a new Collective Labor Agreement for Defense. The biggest change is the new termination of service regulation, which links the retirement age to the AOW (state pension) age. Military personnel will now be dismissed five years before the AOW age. Working longer is no longer only the norm for civilian personnel, but also for military personnel. In 2017, the shortage of personnel (technical and operational) was painfully felt, resulting in many temporary transfers and replacements to meet the required deployment. The frequent transfers led to unrest, and in some cases, it was a reason for departure. To break this downward trend, it was decided to allow only voluntary replacements and to work on extending the duration of assignments where possible. Career Guidance Career guidance is the alignment of personnel wishes with the possibilities that the organization offers regarding career paths. This alignment takes place in the form of a career conversation, which is held during each function or once every three years. This conversation encompasses the personal developments of the involved official in the near future, as well as in the medium and long term. Personal development of the employee is necessary to remain valuable to the organization. In addition to this internal mobility, the career counselor pays attention to external mobility for employees who will not progress in the long term but will leave Defense. The career guidance section included four military offices for the operational service groups, Marines, technical service, and logistics service, and one office for civilian personnel. At the beginning of 2017, this section had 37 military and 3 civilian positions. Since mid-year, the career guidance office for civilian personnel has been fully staffed, allowing for career conversations for civilian personnel on a larger scale. Furthermore, as of October 1, career guidance for civilian personnel has been implemented and established across Defense. The crew of Zr.Ms. Evertse conducts a high-end warfare training during the FOST.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.6)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-6 25 Directorate of Personnel and Operations This year, various groups experienced personnel shortages. This was particularly evident among the junior officers and the middle management of the non-commissioned officers. The 'Technical Allowance' introduced in 2016 was applied unchanged this year, meaning that technical personnel in the rank of corporal to and including warrant officer receive a retention bonus under certain conditions. The idea is that a retention bonus over multiple years will have more effect than the usual one or two years. Another implemented measure for personnel retention is that the 'recycling' of this personnel should be kept to a minimum. An excessively high number of first lieutenants of the Marines and corporals of the Technical Service has been maintained to eventually fill the shortage in the next higher ranks. 2017 presented many challenges for Personnel and Organization (P&O). Everything was done by the staff to contribute maximally to "Safety at and from the sea" by placing the right people, with the right training, in the right positions. Integration (INT) The Integration department (INT) is part of the Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DPBV), one of the three line directorates of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). The INT department aims to manage the operational and supporting process chains of the CZSK integrally on behalf of C-ZSK, focused on delivering deployable units in accordance with the assignment of the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS). The INT department consists of three bureaus: Bureau Strategy and Advice (S&A), Bureau Policy, Planning & Budgeting (BPB), and Bureau Investments (INV). Bureau Strategy & Advice The Bureau S&A supports C-ZSK in its role as maritime military advisor to the CDS and the Minister of Defence. Bureau S&A operates in two teams: the Advice team and the International Military Cooperation team. The Advice team acts as the first point of contact (mailbox) for the Executive Staff (Defence Staff and Main Directorates) regarding policy documents, studies, parliamentary matters, and the so-called Hague consultations. Important tasks this year included activities related to DOKM and the Defence Memorandum. This team also supported the Head of the Policy Directorate in the development of the 'Work Program Maritime Strategy & Ports 2018-2021', an interdepartmental work program initiated together with the Maritime Cluster based on the Maritime Strategy 2015 - 2025. Additionally, this team provides analysis of inspection reports from the Inspector General of the Armed Forces regarding visits to CZSK units. The International Military Cooperation (IMS) team supports C-ZSK in maintaining its international contacts and working relationships.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.7)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-7 26 Directorate of Personnel and Operations in collaboration with the Defense Staff (IMS). In addition to the preparations for regular meetings within the framework of the Belgian-Dutch cooperation (BENESAM) and the Naval Steering Group (NSG) with Germany, an important step has been taken in Dutch-German cooperation. Regarding the operational integration of the German Sea Battalion into the Marine Corps, the Initial Operational Capability of the first mission sets (Force Protection, Very Shallow Water Diving MCM, Non-combatant Evacuation Operations) was achieved on September 22, 2017. A cooperation agreement in the field of submarine search, escape, and rescue has been signed with Sweden, allowing collaboration in the execution of escape exercises using a Swedish rescue submarine. Bureau Policy Planning & Budgeting The Bureau BPB is the first point of contact for the Defense Staff regarding the BPB cycle and the Commandant of the Armed Forces' Directive on Readiness (AGCDS). Bureau BPB is composed of three sections: Planning Integration (PLINT), Programs (PROG), and Material Support (MOST). The PLINT section is responsible for the integral planning process within CZSK. Due to financial constraints, PLINT proposed several measures at the beginning of 2017, in close collaboration with F&C and the AR, to enable more hiring in 2017. The Defense Staff has urged throughout the year to obtain sufficient financial space to address existing backlogs in the supply chain logistics (logistics debt). This space was subsequently also offered to CZSK, after which the Directorate of Material Maintenance (DMI) was able to make significant progress in 2017 and actually overachieved on the budget. In preparing the business plan for 2018/2019, a deepening was carried out on the activities; these are now provided with a (primary) action owner and, moreover, formulated more concretely in many cases. An integration of the short-term activities from the Sailplan 2030 CZSK into the Business Plan also followed, allowing progress to be monitored through the regular Business Reports. The structure of the Business Reports was significantly changed in 2017. Furthermore, the directorates no longer prepare their own reports as input for the CZSK business report, but provide direct input for the CZSK report itself. In this way, the volume of reporting per quarter was halved, and the administrative burden was also reduced. In the Implementation Note, attention was requested from the Executive Staff for the structural shortfall in maintenance, the shortages in various personnel allowances, and the structural lack of staffing space for students in initial training (unavailability for function) as input for the BPB process 2019.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.8)
sections.text: 4_Navy_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS 27 Directorate Personnel and Operations The Programming section is responsible for drafting the Readiness Plan (GSP). This GSP is the long-term plan of the CZSK and looks approximately ten years ahead. It forms the basis for various sub-plans within the CZSK, including the Maintenance Plan of the DMI, the Operational Year Plan of the DOPS, the Filling Plan of P&O, and the Training Plan of the Royal Netherlands Navy Training (OKM). This year, the development proved to be a dynamic process in which all parties involved had to regularly adapt flexibly to rapidly changing environmental factors, which affected both the GSP and the various sub-plans. The integration of maintenance capacity for the Portuguese M-frigates and the prolonged unavailability of various units due to technical problems are examples of this. The responsibility for planning and monitoring the material exploitation lies with the MOST section. In 2017, the section was closely involved in the first defense-wide synchronized Supply and Demand Management (VAM) cycle. Additionally, both internally and externally, efforts were made to improve the VAM structure and processes. Under the leadership of the CDS, contributions were made to further develop and numerically populate the Defense Exploitation Plan – Weapon Systems (DEP-W). The inventory of C-systems that is in use by CZSK, which started in 2016, was completed this year. This inventory serves as input for a military-wide inventory of C-systems, allowing for better budget allocation to address the bottlenecks in the replacement of such systems. The expansion of the section with Project Coordinators for New Material has been accelerated in the context of DOKM. The Project Coordinators will be intensively involved in preparing the CZSK organization for the arrival of new material, which is planned in the various replacement projects within DOKM. Also, this Armory at the Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks.

sections.text: 31 The Directorate of Personnel and Operations was supported by the management group role 2 Chief Medical and Personnel Care (HPGZ). Initially, EGB Carib provided the medical support, but soon units flown in from the Netherlands took over to ensure that the health centers in Curaçao and Aruba would not face capacity issues. On the first flight to Curaçao, part of the Marine Spearhead Task Unit (MSTU) accompanied a doctor. After a few days, a dedicated HPG member followed. Zr.Ms. Zeeland was already present in the Caribbean, and its medical personnel primarily provided support for the command post in Sint Maarten. After Hurricane Maria passed, it became clear that Dominica was also severely affected, prompting Zeeland to relocate to this island and perform 48 medical evacuations for the local population. sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-18 37 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Two of the four diving doctors were transferred at the end of 2017. The personnel plan did not account for a timely replacement of these two diving doctors. Given the training duration of a diving doctor (an average of 18 months), this will lead to problems in the future, considering the disproportionately high workload for the doctors who were not transferred. In addition to the increased workload, they must support any new "diving doctors in training." A similar problem existed with the diving medical nurses. Given the relatively larger pool of this type of personnel, the effects of this issue seemed milder; however, due to frequent changes among diving medical nurses and the need to train specialists, this placed significant pressure on the qualitative filling and support capabilities of the Diving Medical Center (DMC). Duty System For the treatment of victims of both Defense and civilian diving accidents, a diving doctor, a diving medical nurse, and a technician are on standby 24/7. Since only two technicians were qualified in 2017, this was a point of concern and a weak link in the diving medical care chain. Inadequate staffing of the diving duty has consequences for the diving activities of the armed forces. Due to this occupancy rate, the DMC decided in 2017 to discontinue 24-hour care for civilian (sport) divers. Equipment The measuring equipment in the examination department (lung function, exercise ergometry) has long been depreciated and is in urgent need of replacement. The procurement process was difficult, and when in December the procurement of new examination equipment finally seemed to be concluded, the remaining supplier did not meet the requirements. Expanding Tasks Despite the above, the DMC was able to deliver more output in scientific areas and support than in previous years. This is the result of a reorganization of personnel and resources and the optimization of operations. Thanks to an employee, a management information system has been established, allowing the DMC to utilize all available capacities more effectively. To align the actual job content with the job descriptions, a reorganization is conceivable in the long term.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.19)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-19 38 Directorate Personnel and Operations Social Medical Service In 2017, the Social Medical Service (SMD) provided occupational health care and personnel support, as part of the reintegration policy of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK), assisting clinical and outpatient patients. This year, a total of 360 military personnel registered with the SMD. The clinical patients primarily consist of military personnel with injuries or ailments related to the musculoskeletal system. They are internally guided to reach the high fitness level of their operational unit, so that they can recover from their injuries and resume their work without falling behind in fitness. The Physical Profile for Marines (FMP) describes the required fitness level per rank and is divided into three levels. The expected physical profile for fleet personnel, who operate together with marines and must meet a higher fitness level than when assigned to the fleet, has not yet been published. Fleet personnel who become unfit are rehabilitated to fitness in accordance with the requirements of the Defense Fitness Test (DCP). The collaboration between the EGB and SMD has taken more shape. Although the SMD Dentist and dental assistant are working in Den Helder.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.20)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-20 39 The Directorate of Personnel and Operations, as an independent unit of CZSK, provides primary occupational health care outside the EGB. This did not lead to any problems. The SMD adheres to the quality requirements of the EGB regarding occupational health care, contributes to the content of new guidelines and work instructions, and consults with the doctors of the EGB on points where care intersects. This is particularly the case during the transfer of absenteeism guidance from the EGB to the SMD when a member of CZSK is absent for more than six weeks or when there is a limitation in deployability. This transfer is documented in the Directive CZSK 410. The proposed closure of the Marine Establishment Amsterdam (MEA) necessitates the relocation of the SMD. Advanced plans in 2016 to move the Service to buildings on the Aardenburg site in Doorn were halted in early 2017. The arrival of the SMD could have a disruptive effect on the patient care of the Military Rehabilitation Center (MRC) there. Efforts were made to seek cooperation in areas such as therapeutic swimming and occupational therapy, but this proved impossible without affecting the working methods of either the MRC or the SMD. The requirements plan was completed in March 2017, and based on that, alternative locations were considered. The Korporaal van Oudheusden Barracks (KVOK) in Hilversum was found to be suitable, and in April 2017, the green light was given for the relocation of the Service to the KVOK. Utilizing existing buildings required extensive modifications, which still did not meet the requirements plan. It was decided to place two new buildings constructed from prefab units on the open grounds of the KVOK where the Marine Examination Center previously stood. This met the required delivery in July 2018, allowing the relocation to begin on time. For the future, cooperation is being sought with, for example, the MRC department of occupational rehabilitation, so that at the end of the lifespan of the prefab housing at KVOK, a new purpose for the SMD is ready. Unfortunately, it became clear that it would not be possible to have the final design ready in time and thus to tender the project. At the beginning of December, it was stated that the delivery of one of the two buildings could perhaps take place on time, but by the end of the year, it became clear that this was also impossible. Additionally, the phased delivery of the two buildings was not feasible without disrupting the training program of the internally placed patients. It is further unclear what the effect of the above will be on the planned closure of the MEA. What is certain is that the SMD cannot relocate in time to vacate the current building by July 1, 2018, for transfer to the project office marine area Amsterdam. Relocation to a temporary location is pending.

Bureau Mental Resilience The Mental Resilience Cluster (MV) is responsible for the Collegial Network Royal Netherlands Navy (CN KM) and stress management. MV focused over the past year on training new Collegial Networkers (CN-ers) and Trauma Risk Management (TRiM) team leaders. This involved ensuring the quality of the already trained CN-ers and embedding the CN KM within the CZSK. The CN KM saw several deployments in 2017 where the TRiM protocol was applied. Quality assurance has taken place, among other things, through skills days and organizing a study day.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.24)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-24 43 Directorate Personnel and Operations In the AGCDS 2018, it is stated that all defense components must implement the Directive 'psychosocial support for uniformed personnel' (Impact directive) by establishing a Collegial Network. CZSK has partially set up this network. There is currently no network for civilian personnel. The MV Bureau has supported other defense components in establishing various networks by opening up training sessions and participation in working groups. As part of stress management, briefings were held in preparation for various missions. Collaboration has been sought with various schools/trainers such as KIM, SMVBO, MOC, Maritime Team Training and Applied Leadership (MTTL), and Netherlands Maritime Special Operations Force (NLMARSOF). Within this collaboration, a way was explored to uniformly offer a stress management tool. NLMARSOF operators are about to jump during an exercise above Leeuwarden.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.25)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-25 44 Directorate Personnel and Operations. To this end, NLMARSOF has initiated the training pilot "Mental Strength." Within this pilot, various stress management tools were offered, including those from sports psychology. The goal of all this is to enhance performance and reduce dropout rates by making participants more resilient. Case Management Office CZSK The office handles individual cases with an irregular character that require special attention and recognition from the employer. Typically, these involve complex care issues that may be politically and/or media-sensitive, have a high risk of failure, are multidisciplinary in nature, and therefore require coordination. The year 2017 was marked by an increase in the number of cases and the corresponding workload per case. The cause of this may be that the functionality of case management is increasingly proving itself or that more and more supervisors and employees are finding their way to the office. Another possible reason for the increase could be the effect of the reorganization on regular processes at centrally allocated services of Defense. This year, the Case Management Office also received several new (alleged) article 4 (employment under special circumstances) reintegrants in its portfolio. Maritime Team Training and Applied Leadership MTTL is a small office with seven FTE, specializing in team training in the maritime-military domain. It provides three 'products' to teams of the CZSK. Since 2013, the focus has shifted from guiding individual leaders to guiding leaders and their teams. The first of these is the Team-APK training, and after the summer of 2017, the new 'Building Trust' team training. These trainings are conducted at an external training location at the Old Rijkswerf in Den Helder. The second product is the Coaching Course for Supervisors CZSK (LCC). In this course, civilian and military supervisors (from the rank of Lieutenant at sea 2nd Class) learn to coach as a form of leadership. The third product involves two MTTL members working on training Crew Resource Management (CRM) instructors for the fleet and marines and guiding teams on CRM. Training CRM instructors is the first step in integrating CRM within all training and education of CZSK. This is done in close cooperation with a Mobile Training Team from the US Navy. The essence of CRM is that, in addition to the usual training of technical skills, teams are viewed in a different, broader way. The collaboration between people and not so much non-technical skills is central to this. The services provided by the MTTL office are adjusted as much as possible to the needs of the teams.

MTTL is continuously engaged in the (further) development of new products. Unfortunately, the planned team training sessions in the West were largely canceled this year due to Hurricane Irma passing over the Leeward Islands. In 2017, collaboration was sought in the area of CRM with the Royal Netherlands Naval College (KIM) and the SMVBO. For the first time, Flag Officer Sea Training (FOST) staff members were guests as students at the Immunization (IMM) CRM training course in November. In 2018, MTTL will continue discussions with FOST on whether CRM can be used as 'the' evaluation tool for non-technical skills throughout the entire operational chain (including FOST). There was also more intensive collaboration with Belgian marine colleagues by opening the LCC and IMM CRM training courses to their leaders. In 2017, approximately 800 personnel from CZSK were trained by MTTL trainers in various training sessions/LCCs. NH90s hunting a submarine during the FOST exercise near Heston, United Kingdom.

One of the measures eligible for additional funding was the strengthening of the training domain. In collaboration with the schools, a plan was developed with three tracks. This year, the AKL was digitized, making it accessible via the Software Application for Standard Reports (COGNOS). Closure of Thetis In September, the decision was made to close the Maritime Training and Exercise Centre with immediate effect. The main reason was that the status of that platform regarding fire safety and working conditions was found to be so poor that further use was no longer responsible. Subsequently, in close collaboration between the Maritime Support Department of the DMI and OKM, an interim solution was established. The DDS was given access to the workshop of the Technical Maintenance Team of 'Klein Bovenwater', which moved to the Submarine Service Complex. Due to the great enthusiasm and effort, especially from DDS staff, this space could be put into use by the end of the year. A project for a definitive replacement of Thetis has been included in the DIP. New Pyromaan. On October 5, the SCBRNDC&BV took the new Pyromaan into use. Under the watchful eye of the Director of Personnel and Operations, Commodore (cdr) R.T. Luyckx, and the Director of Material Maintenance, Commander (cdr) P. Knipping, the commander of the SCBRNDCBV, Lieutenant Commander (kltz) R.N.A. Gans, declared the building to be in use. The commissioning was symbolized by the unveiling of a plaque with the names of the first crew members of the building. The plaque was unveiled by the two corporals, A. Lenstra and J. Reekers, who had to stay the longest in the temporary emergency building. The new Pyromaan replaces two outdated training objects; the breathing apparatus course and the Medical Action Service (MAD) moot. Additionally, the building contains a more modern laundry and storage for firefighting clothing. Furthermore, it has an improved shower and changing area, which supports cleaner working conditions. Finally, the office and recreation areas are located on the top floor, providing a good overview of the complex and thus making a significant contribution to safety.

sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-35 54 Directorate of Personnel and Operations The Belgian-Dutch catering school (CCSp Dept Catering BENL) Commandant: Major R. Dejaghere Commandant NL-DET: Lieutenant (junior grade) (SD) H.C.M. Feitsma From October 26, Lieutenant (junior grade) (LD) R. Vervelde In 2017, the continued existence of the school was under scrutiny. On the Belgian side, restructuring took place, during which the catering concept was also examined. Given the potentially far-reaching consequences for the training of Belgian catering personnel, consideration was given to the possible outsourcing of the training to civilian parties. This approach proved unfeasible; the timeframe in which the school could prepare students for their (Defense) tasks was much shorter than that of a civilian trainer. The company restaurant at the barracks in Bruges sought collaboration with the school in 2017. Initially driven by personnel challenges, but also from the perspective of the school, the company restaurant seemed a welcome opportunity to better simulate everyday practice. The initial experiences raised some points of attention, but the agreement followed to continue this initiative in the coming period. At the request of the coast guard, the school trained cooks for Aruba. Thus, it fulfilled the concept of 'learning everywhere and always.' The involved trainer, who was familiar with the workings on the island, was able to provide customized training, tailored to the prior knowledge of the student cooks, with the program focused on the specific situation of the galley aboard a cutter. This process resulted in well-deserved certificates with social significance. The civil qualification of Dutch sailors and prospective corporals increasingly demands more from the training time. While the school had previously faced additional requirements in the areas of mathematics, English, and Dutch (REN subjects), attention is now being requested within the Secondary Vocational Education for so-called 'elective components.' These training programs provide the necessary broadening or deepening of the fixed curriculum for level 2 and level 3 training. In consultation with ROC Midden Nederland, the school sought to determine where these elective components could be integrated into the existing training content, so that additional training time was minimized. In co-creation, elective components have now been developed, and another is on the horizon.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.37)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-37 56 Directorate Personnel and Operations This year, the SCBRNDCBV has also focused on filling long-standing vacancies by attracting and internally training new instructors. They will further develop their skills during their placement. Additionally, personnel from elsewhere within the CZSK, who may be interested in following the internal instructor training (UA04), have been sought. Through modernization in equipment with two new simulator trainers, realistic training can be conducted in the 'one-line extinguishing technique', which reduces water consumption for firefighting. The nozzle trainer, which can simulate a hot gas layer using gas (the layer of hot air that rises during a fire and eventually ignites), is functioning properly and is an important component of the training simulators. The fire progression trainer (flash-over trainer) is also being extensively used. A significant advantage of the new simulator trainers is that they are equipped with a post-combustion system, allowing training to occur under nearly all meteorological conditions and resulting in less environmental impact. School for Maritime Education and Operations (SMVBO) Commander: kltz R.M. Platel This year, the Intake Department ensured that out of the 326 enrolled EMMV students, 268 successfully completed this training. For the Flow Department, the year 2017 was primarily focused on facilitating the renewed training programs. In 2016, significant substantive changes were implemented within the SMVBO-Flow training programs. For instance, the Management Training Course (LMV) structure was overhauled, reducing the total number of LMVs from eight to six, and these programs are now tied to a specific rank and career path. This meant that starting this year, following an LMV was no longer voluntary but a mandatory part of the career path to be followed. After a year full of innovation, the time had come to reap the benefits of this, and despite a shortage of trainers, a significant number of training programs were conducted. The Flow Department trained 1690 out of 1744 registered participants, spread over 149 training programs.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.38)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-38 57 Directorate Personnel and Operations Defense Diving Group & Defense Diving School (DDG & DDS) Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) B.A. Visser Diving Company It was an operationally interesting year for the diving company of the DDG. The diving teams participated in the large-scale exercises Western Partnership in the Caribbean waters, Northern Coasts in the Baltic Sea, and Bold Alligator in the Atlantic Ocean. Furthermore, various diving teams were deployed in the Dutch waters. In Den Helder, for example, the DDG participated in the exercise Sandy Coast, which focused on mine countermeasures. Additionally, the exercise Port Defender in Rotterdam required cooperation among all safety and assistance organizations. The exercise took an unexpected turn when a human remains was discovered and recovered. The DDG was also active in terms of military assistance. There were several deployments where divers searched for missing persons in collaboration with the National Underwater Search Team (LTOZ) of the police. The DDG concluded the year in Delfzijl with the port protection exercise Joint Protector in cooperation with the local police and port authorities. Divers from the Defense Diving Group at work during the exercise Port Defender in Rotterdam.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.39)
sections.text: 4_Navy_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-39 58 Directorate Personnel and Operations Training Institution Defense Diving School The training institution DDS consists of three training units: 'Diving, Underwater Weapons and Explosives', 'Specialist Operations', and 'Diving Medicine', as well as the bureau 'Training & Education'. In addition to executing the regular training calendar, where divers, dive leaders, and diving medical personnel were trained or retrained for the four Operational Commands (CZSK, CLAS, CLSK, and KMar), external partners, including the police, customs, the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science (OC&W), and the civil sector, were also able to utilize the available residual capacity in the training programs. The year was also marked by the implementation of the BGO. For this, the staffing of the educational developers increased to 100%, employees followed the necessary training, a guidance structure for instructors was established, and work began on structuring the learning pathways according to this system. Additionally, an organizational scan was conducted due to a discrepancy that had arisen between the required and available capacity. In 2018, efforts will begin to address this. To operationalize the unused IS-MIX diving system (a diving system designed for mine countermeasures) again, the training units and the bureau Training & Education started providing retraining courses. At the end of the year, the DDS faced a setback when it had to close the Thetis for safety reasons due to overdue maintenance. However, the requirement for the replacement of this Maritime Training and Exercise Center was already in progress and is expected to be realized by mid-2020. Certifying Institution Knowledge & Quality Defense Diving School In the area of personnel certification, personnel from Defense, police, customs, fire department, and the Ministry of OCW were certified again this year. The knowledge center conducted tests to validate dive tables suitable for diving with a rebreather diving system to a depth of 81 meters. Since regular air in the atmosphere becomes toxic at these depths, a breathing gas mixture of helium and oxygen (HELIOX) must be used at greater depths. The tests involved collaboration with institutions in Canada, Sweden, and Australia.

Development, innovation, and projects
In addition to the core business of the KMTO, which is training students in technology, the school works on its own development. For instance, its personnel are certified. Instructors and educational development teams follow ECOD training to ensure their skills remain at the appropriate level. Furthermore, work is being done within the school on the development of training equipment and training environments. In 2017, for example, new test boards were developed for the Refrigeration Technology department, and the updated Datalink training was given for the first time. Datalink involves sending information over the network. The training was updated because the old Datalink equipment on board the ships is being replaced with new material. The boat is an excellent BGO learning tool and is used for the training 'FRISC Maintenance Provider', which was conducted thirteen times by the unit in 2017. This year's training took place in Belize, which presents a significant challenge regarding communications due to the dense vegetation and the unpredictable nature of the terrain. NIMCIS Very High Frequency (VHF) and Ultra High Frequency (UHF) are virtually unusable here, making reliance solely on HF communications necessary. In response to the concerning situation regarding these communications during the last training in Belize in 2015, the JKCMOX requested extensive communication tests to be conducted in the various training areas in Belize. Therefore, the HF Test Team (HFTT), consisting of eight personnel, successfully tested and mapped the HF communications over a period of fourteen days. The goal was to ensure that tactical and safety communications could be maintained throughout at least JW(I)C 2017 by thoroughly testing HF communications both day and night. With the necessary improvements and solutions implemented, the creation of a Standard Operations Procedure (SOP) for "communications in a jungle environment" is currently in progress. sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-9 84 The Operations Directorate oversees naval units and the Coast Guard Cutters in the Caribbean region and additionally provides support to the fleet and NATO allies. The STC consists of six departments: GBW, Submarine Service, Mine Countermeasures Vessels Mine Operational Sea Training (M(CMV)OST), Force Protection and Boarding Operations (FPBO), Weapons System Management (WSM GBW), and STC-Shore. The Shore department comprises the Ship Operations Bureau (SBV), the Bureau for Consolidation, Preparation, and Sustainability (CG&B), and the Safety and Environment Bureau (V&M). Sea Training Command: Shore In 2017, five larger naval units began their operational training trajectory. After completing their SARC-1 and SARC-2, these units were further trained at sea by the GBW department or the MOST. For the smaller units, including tugs, training, diving, and landing craft, the transition to the PvB system has commenced. This involves separating the training of the crew from the platform. Ten of these smaller platforms have been delivered as operationally ready, and twenty personnel have obtained their PvB certification. Even during the operational period of the units, they are monitored and corrected where necessary. Five so-called CTs have been conducted, part of which took place in the West. Additionally, thirty-one readiness checks have been carried out to assess whether the units still meet the high standards established during their training trajectory. For four units, it was determined after inspection that the operations were sufficiently in order to commence scheduled maintenance and then resume the training trajectory. Finally, ten major safety presentations were given on location as part of various P-weeks, and a contribution was made to five VMS-Def training courses. Captain (ktz) A.S. Warnaar (EMSD) Commander Sea Training Command.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.10)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-10 85 Operations Directorate Sea Training Command: Submarine Service In 2017, Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw, the first IPW boat, underwent a complete training trajectory. Additionally, operational support was provided to Zr.Ms. Bruinvis and a Pre-Deployment Training (PDT) was conducted on board Zr.Ms. Walrus. For both operational and training missions, a total of seventeen Towed Array deployment and recovery operations were carried out domestically and abroad. For both operational and training missions, a total of fourteen Towed Array coupling actions and recovery operations were conducted. Sea Training Command: Major Surface Units (GBW) In 2017, the STC prepared nine ships to different levels. A total of fourteen weeks were spent at sea to conduct various SARC and PDT exercises. In the first month of the year, the training trajectory of Zr.Ms. Evertsen was completed through a Staff Sea Check and a SARC 4. This training period was largely conducted in the exercise areas of the FOST near Plymouth. The sparring partner for this period was Zr.Ms. Groningen. Intensive training was conducted with foreign units that were also undergoing a training trajectory at FOST. All warfare types were practiced. Both ships made a port visit to Southampton over the weekend. During this port visit, the ties between the Dutch Navy and the British community were strengthened through a party on board Zr.Ms. Evertsen. After the success, the NH90 conducted a deck landing on the helideck of Zr.Ms. Groningen.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.11)
sections.text: The Operations Directorate completed the SARC-4 for Zr.Ms. Evertsen, which was declared exercise-ready by C-STC. Shortly thereafter, STC provided support for a limited CT trajectory of Zr.Ms. Van Amstel as a supplement to the regular PDT planned before departure to the West. After Zr.Ms. Evertsen and Zr.Ms. Van Amstel, it was Zr.Ms. Zeeland's turn in March to complete its training trajectory. This also took place in the form of a Staff Sea Check and a SARC-4. Unlike Zr.Ms. Evertsen, Zr.Ms. Zeeland and its sparring partner Zr.Ms. Groningen conducted the training trajectory in Danish waters. Several exercises were carried out with units from the Danish national reserve and units from the Danish Navy. Highlights included exercises on the MULTEX range and a disaster response exercise near the town of Albaeck. During the intervening weekend, a port visit was made to the Danish town of Aarhus. Zr.Ms. Zeeland was also declared exercise-ready by C-STC. After successfully completing the SARC-5 & 6 at FOST, Zr.Ms. Zeeland was declared organically operationally ready and underwent another PDT on its way to the West, after which the vessel was also mission-specific ready for its role as Station Ship Caribbean Area (SSCG). The shooting line is being crossed for a RAS between Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman and Zr.Ms. De Ruyter in the North Sea.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.12)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-12 87 Operations Directorate From May 8 to 16, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman was the next ship to undergo maintenance by STC. Due to circumstances, this was the 3rd SARC-3 for the ship in the past four years. The warship had previously been deployed early for an extraordinary mission and had to deal with a serious propulsion problem, which meant it could never fully complete its regular training trajectory. This SARC-3 was taken up after a long repair period of both Main Electric Motors (HEM). The ship was trained in basic safety procedures and damage control. After completing the SARC-3, the sailing readiness status was confirmed again. May also saw STC-GBW focused on the training of Zr.Ms. Van Speyk. Together with her partner ship Zr.Ms. De Ruyter, both vessels departed on May 27 towards the south of Great Britain to the South Coast Exercise Areas for a SARC-4 program. This exercise area was chosen again because a balanced and specific training program can be developed there for warships in cooperation with FOST. Since Zr.Ms. Van Speyk was equipped with the Low Frequency Active and Passive Sonar (LFAPS) sonar system, a specific training program was developed with an emphasis on anti-submarine warfare. Unfortunately, since the involved submarine was withdrawn early, STC largely reverted to the standard trajectory. Over the weekend, both ships paid a port visit to Portsmouth. After two intensive training weeks, both ships, with an opposed entry, returned to the port of Den Helder on June 2. During an All Hands, C-STC informed the crew that the ship was training-ready and could continue its training trajectory. After successfully completing SARC 5 & 6 with FOST, Zr.Ms. Van Speyk was declared operationally ready and, on her departure to the West, underwent a PDT after which she was also mission-specific ready for her role as SSCG. On June 11, STC-GBW, again with support from the SCBRNDCBV school (OPOE team), KMTO, and DMI, departed from Zeebrugge for a PDT of BNS Louise-Marie. The ship received training in preparation for her mission in the Mediterranean Sea, Operation Sophia. This mission aims to combat human smuggling and arms trafficking in the eastern part of the Mediterranean Sea. Up to Malaga, the PDT focused on fire and damage control, after which the training became more mission-specific. After a staff change in Malaga, the ship set course towards the east of Sicily to conduct a boarding exercise with the Italian Navy. Along the way, exercises were conducted in intercepting refugees, deploying the Fire Support Team, handling prisoners, and training the boarding team. The crew also practiced flight operations with the deployed...

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.14)
sections.text: Directie Operaties embarked Allouette III. On June 20, the staff debarked in Augusta, after which the ship was ready for its mission. After the summer leave, the staff embarked on board Zr.Ms. Rotterdam to also conduct a PDT with this ship. This training was carried out during the outbound journey to the Anti-Piracy mission Atalanta. For this, several enablers were embarked, including a Cougar helicopter from the 300 Squadron DHC, a Swedish Enhanced Boarding Element (EBE), an EBE from the Corps of Marines, a Swedish CB90 squadron, three FRISC’s from SATG, and an ART. Since all these modules needed to be prepared for the mission, a diverse staff was assembled consisting of personnel from KMTO, DMI, the SCBRNDCBV school, MTC, Defence Intelligence and Security Institute (DIVI), Defence Helicopter Command (DHC), and MHKC. The first part of the PDT focused on fire, damage control, and the individual preparation of the enablers. After the staff change in Malaga, the focus shifted to the mission and the integration of the enablers. A transit to Malta followed, where a two-day exercise program took place with the Maltese Defence Force. After part of the staff was dropped off in La Valetta, Malta, the ship continued its journey towards Crete to conduct two large boarding exercises at the NATO Maritime Interdiction Operations Training Centre (NMIOTC). After this, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was ready for its mission and continued its journey towards Port Said. While part of the staff conducted the PDT on Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, another part of the staff embarked on Sunday, September 3, on board Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman to commence SARC-4. After Karel Doorman departed from Rotterdam, a rendezvous was made with units of the Dutch task group, which was under the command of MBS NLMARFOR. Together, they practiced seamanship and navigation skills. The Belgian NH90 helicopter embarked on board practiced with the Dutch ships and conducted dual spot operations with a Dutch NH90 from Zr.Ms. Van Amstel on board Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman. The entire squadron set course for the Swedish Karlskrona for the Pre SAIL conference of the Northern Coasts exercise. In Karlskrona, the rest of the STC staff, who had previously supported the PDT of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, boarded. With a complete staff, the ship departed on Monday, September 11, along with all other units, for the Northern Coasts exercise at sea. After two days of intensive training, the ship was recalled to the Netherlands to take on supplies and provide support to the Windward Islands, which had been affected by Hurricane Irma. Due to this change of mission, the ship could not complete its SARC-4. The last two deployments of the year 2017 were twice a SARC-3 of respect.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.15)
sections.text:
The Operations Directorate faced challenges with Zr.Ms. Friesland and Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt. Both units were plagued by material shortcomings, resulting in a difficult start. However, through combined efforts, the SARC-3 for both units was concluded with a satisfactory result. Both vessels were therefore declared ready for sailing in a timely manner. The year was to be concluded with two training periods, the CT for Zr.Ms. Holland and the SARC-4 for Zr.Ms. Friesland. Due to class-wide issues with the water mist installation of the patrol vessel, both ships were unable to complete their training trajectory. Support for the ACT(ASW) of Zr.Ms. Van Amstel also could not proceed due to technical problems. 

Sea Training Command: MOST 

MOST provided training for 27 units from eight different countries during 58 sailing weeks in 2017. The mobile MOST team was deployed four times in four different countries in 2017. The year began with the CT for BNS Primula, while the Sea Acceptance Trials (SATs) and the SARC 3 for Zr.Ms. Makkum were conducted simultaneously. In early February, MOST provided support to Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group 1 (SNMCMG) while it was in Zeebrugge. During this execution, two Italian seariders from La Spezia were guests at MOST as observers. At the end of February, a CT for BNS Godetia was conducted, and training was provided for Willemstad. Subsequently, CTs for Zr.Ms. Snellius, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen, and BNS Lobelia were conducted. The mobile team underwent an extended Fast Cruise (FC) of Zr.Ms. Mercuur in week 13 in Den Helder. An extended FC was necessary because the Varende Materieels Beproevingen (VMBs) commenced immediately after extensive maintenance and significant propulsion modifications. 

At the beginning of spring, the SARC 3 and 4 for Zr.Ms. Luymes were scheduled, while the other team conducted the CT for BNS Narcis. Immediately after, the FC and VMBs for Zr.Ms. Urk were on the agenda. In May, a NATO test of the Latvian ship Virsaitis was planned; for its execution, a mobile team flew to Liepaja, Latvia. At the same time, the other team was deployed in Zeebrugge for the execution of the SARC-3 of Zr.Ms. Mercuur, followed by the SARC-3 of Zr.Ms. Urk and the VMBs of BNS Bellis. On June 6, the German minehunter Sulzbach Rosenberg was present in Zeebrugge for a NATO test. The other training team conducted a CT for BNS Castor and BNS Bellis.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.16)
sections.text:
On June 18, the mobile team was deployed to Tallinn to conduct a NATO test with the Sakala. The time leading up to the leave was further filled with a SARC-4 for Zr.Ms. Mercuur and a CT for BNS Lobelia. After the leave, work began on the SARC-5 and -6 for Zr.Ms. Makkum, while support was provided to STC Shore for the upgrade of Zr.Ms. Pelikaan and the Jaguar from Curaçao. During those training sessions, the Swedish naval commander Rear Admiral Jens Nykvist paid a two-day working visit to MOST. The support for the upgrade of Zr.Ms. Pelikaan was canceled due to the ship's deployment in the West following the damage caused by Hurricane Irma. On September 25, a MOST team began the SARC-5 and -6 for Zr.Ms. Urk. Subsequently, a mobile team departed for Kiel to subject the FGS Bad Rappenau to a NATO test. At the same time, the other MOST team subjected the Lithuanian minehunter Kursis to a NATO test in Zeebrugge. The year concluded with the execution of CTs for BNS Bellis and BNS Pollux. 

Maritime Headquarters ABNL 
The Maritime Headquarters ABNL (MHK ABNL) is part of the Operations Directorate of the CZSK. The MHK is responsible for Belgian and Dutch operations and exercises of fleet and marine units. The MHK ABNL: Programs, plans, directs, coordinates, and supports operational readiness activities. Prepares mandated operations, executes them, and supports these operations. Prepares operations on behalf of the CDS and supports them. Provides general advice on maritime military operations. Drafts the bi-national operational year plan (OJP) and oversees the realization of the assigned activities. Additionally, the MHK ABNL serves as the 24/7 point of contact and coordination within CZSK for operational matters.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.17)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-17 92 Directorate Operations Operational Units Fleet Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt Commander: Captain (ktz) W.L. van Zanten In the summer of 2017, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt came out of Designated Maintenance and the crew was placed on board. This was followed by a long training period, with SARC-2 and -3 under the leadership of STC in October and the VMB in November. Zr.Ms. Rotterdam Commander: Captain (ktz) H.H. Liebregs On March 24, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam departed for Vlissingen for the CERTIFEX aimed at training the 22 Raiding Squadron to MARC 4 and MARSOC level. For this purpose, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was equipped with two Cougars. The exercise was conducted near Vlissingen, Texel, and at the Marnewaard. As a Ready Duty Ship (RDS), Zr.Ms. Rotterdam went to sea on King's Day to escort a Russian frigate in the North Sea. May 9 was marked by the skills day for Recruitment and Selection, followed by the MARVO Skills Day on May 10. Subsequently, the ship made its first foreign port visit of the year to Portsmouth. In this British port city, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam provided support for the preparations for the ceremonial first entry of the new carrier HMS Queen Elizabeth. Following this, from May 15 to 18, the WET-FEET exercise took place for the First Military Training of the Marine Corps. On Friday, May 19, the families of the crew were thanked with a sailing family day. The families were embarked using landing craft while the ship was anchored in the roadstead of Den Helder. On June 23, 24, and 25, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was designated to participate in the Marine Days, which this year coincided with SAIL Den Helder. The ship also contributed in collaboration with Amazon and the Den Helder Suns. In addition to the usual tour on board, visitors could play the latest e-game from Amazon, there were basketball and laser game fields set up, and racing simulations were provided.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.18)
sections.text: Directie Operaties From June 29 to July 7, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam departed to sea for helicopter trials (Vlicozee), the Practical Training for Officer of the Marines (POTOM), and the Helicopter Qualification Week. From July 10 to July 17, the exercise CERTIFEX was conducted for the training of the 13 Raiding Squadron. The summer leave followed in week 30 through week 32. Immediately after, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam prepared for departure to the Somali basin for the anti-piracy mission EUNAVFOR Somalia. On Sunday, August 27, the ship set sail with its crew. The permanent crew of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was supplemented with a Role 2, 300 squadron, marines with an amphibious team and a boarding team, a Swedish detachment with an amphibious team and a boarding team of Swedish marines, a sniper, intelligence personnel, and interpreters. In addition to the personnel reinforcement, extra equipment was present, including a Cougar, FRISCs, and two Swedish CB-90s. The first two weeks were focused on pre-deployment training under the leadership of STC. Subsequently, the ship was deemed operationally ready by C-STC after which they disembarked in Crete. After passing through the Suez Canal, the mission officially commenced under the leadership of an Italian staff. From September 30 to October 28, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was off the coast of Somalia.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.19)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-19 94 The Operations Directorate was tasked with executing operation AEOLUS. This operation was aimed at gathering intelligence to be used for a key leader engagement. The first phase took place off the northern coast of Somaliland/Puntland and then proceeded south along the coast of Somalia. Just before the first port visit in the Seychelles, Neptunus and Neptunia boarded to 'baptize' the 'waves' while crossing the equator. Subsequently, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam anchored off Port Victoria. The second part of the mission was also focused on operation AEOLUS. After that, the port of Mombasa was visited where the local authorities hosted a reception. On Saturday, October 14, two bomb attacks occurred in Mogadishu resulting in over 800 dead and injured. Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was asked to investigate whether medical support was possible. Discussions were held at Mogadishu International Airport with representatives from local hospitals. Zr.Ms. Rotterdam then provided the necessary aid supplies. From November 1 to 5, Salalah, Oman, was visited for resupply and rest and recreation for the crew. The transit from Salalah to Djibouti was focused on conducting friendly approaches. On November 13, the mission officially came to an end. In Djibouti, VPD packages were loaded for transport to the Netherlands. The journey continued through the Suez Canal to Lisbon, where the ship arrived on November 26. On November 29, the journey continued to the home port of Den Helder, where Zr.Ms. Rotterdam arrived on Sunday, December 3. After a short disembarkation leave, the ship prepared for the scheduled maintenance period and a sustainment program following the winter leave. Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman Commander: Captain (ktz) S.L. Schot At the beginning of 2017, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman was still docked in Den Helder, waiting for the reinstallation of the starboard HEM. The port side HEM had been reinstalled at the end of 2016 due to a defect. In January, the ship hosted the traditional New Year's run and dive of the entire Nieuwe Haven. Later that month, a detachment formed an honor guard during the visit of the Chief of Defence of New Zealand to The Hague. The ship was also visited as part of the working visit by the European faction of the CDA and by a delegation from the Indonesian navy.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.20)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-20 95 Operations Directorate At the beginning of February, the first "warm" test was conducted on the port HEM; the Harbour Acceptance Test (HAT). This day coincided with SARC 1. The ship also hosted the TECH information day and received a visit from a delegation of the Karel Doorman Fund Foundation. On February 17, the starboard HEM arrived in Den Helder, after which the process of reinstallation began immediately. On February 27, a crew detachment was present in The Hague during the commemoration of the Battle of the Java Sea, and during a similar commemoration at Museum Bronbeek in Arnhem. The commander, Captain (ktz) S.L. Schot, was also present at a commemoration of the Battle of the Java Sea later that week at the Karel Doorman monument at the Dutch war cemetery Kembang Kuning in Surabaya, Indonesia. The training program continued with the Slow Cruise and the FT on April 19, after which the ship set sail on April 20 for the first time since both HEMs were reinstalled, to conduct SAT. It was a positive boost for the enthusiastic crew that everything was functioning properly again. Subsequently, under the leadership of STC, SARC-3 was conducted, during which the ship made a brief port visit to Southampton. At the beginning of May, a crew delegation attended a memorial service at the National War Cemetery in Loenen. During this period, the ship received a visit from the Association of Former Officers of the Technical and Electrical Service. It then departed again to sea to conduct maritime equipment trials. At the beginning of June, the ship sailed towards Norway to perform some tests near Bergen. After conducting these tests, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman made a brief port visit to Haakonsvern, after which it returned to Den Helder for the next event; the Marine Days. It was the first time the ship was open to the public during the Marine Days. The event coincided with SAIL, and the ship also hosted the Captain's Dinner. During these days, over 20,600 visitors were welcomed on board. After the Marine Days, the next guests were already on the quay, as the ship, in the context of a previously signed Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Germany, served as the base for a three-week anti-terror exercise by German Special Forces. The Germans brought along a civil target ship and two types of helicopters to Den Helder; the Sikorsky Sea King and a Sikorsky CH53. The ship was at the World Port Days in Rotterdam during the last weekend of August. It was the second time for the ship, and this time it was also prominently located at the Holland Amerikakade. Before arriving in Rotterdam, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman conducted the re-

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.21)
sections.text: Directorate Operations organized a maritime day for CZSK. Approximately 600 guests witnessed the operational capabilities during a demonstration of oil loading with Zr.Ms. Holland. In Rotterdam itself, the ship supported the opening reception of the World Port Days with several prominent visitors and a Reservists Employers Day. Onboard, the promotion of Prince Maurits to Captain (ktz) of the Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve took place. Additionally, the ship was open to the public and received over 12,000 visitors onboard. After these busy days, the ship set sail again to participate in the Northern Coasts exercise in the Baltic Sea. At the same time, the vessel was prepared under the guidance of STC. What was planned as a five-week voyage with a large Dutch squadron turned out differently when the ship received orders to return to Den Helder. Due to the hurricane season and the damage caused by Hurricane Irma on the island of Sint Maarten and other Windward Islands, the ship immediately joined Zr.Ms. Zeeland and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan to provide emergency assistance in the West. The ship arrived on September 15 in Den Helder, loading Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman with aid supplies for Sint Maarten.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.22)
sections.text: Operations Directorate Helder, after which efforts were made with all hands to be able to depart on Wednesday, September 20. The Karel Doorman departed towards Portsmouth to pick up several containers of emergency aid destined for the British Virgin Islands. After that, it began the crossing towards the West, where it docked in the port of Philipsburg, Sint Maarten at the beginning of October. The offloading of the aid supplies was received with great interest from Prime Minister W. Marlin, Governor E.B. Holiday, CZMCARIB Brigadier General of Marines P.J. de Vin, and other local government officials, citizens, and press. The offloading of the brought goods went smoothly; the entire ship was unloaded within 24 hours. Various dignitaries were received, such as the Commissioner of Sint Eustatius J. Woodley and the outgoing Minister of the Interior and Kingdom Relations R.H.A. Plasterk. Several crew members were deployed locally under the leadership of the Royal Netherlands Army to clear debris. The ship conducted a Replenishment In Port (RIP) with the British RFA Mounts Bay. In addition to fuel, the brought aid supplies for the British Virgin Islands were transferred. After the first offload, the ship departed again to sea to steam towards Dominica, the island that had suffered extensive damage from Hurricane Maria. A team of technical personnel remained in Sint Maarten to assist the army with operations. After delivering water for the population in Dominica, the ship embarked aid supplies in nearby Guadeloupe. After dropping off these goods in Dominica, the Karel Doorman returned to Sint Maarten, after which it set course towards the ABC islands. In Curaçao and Aruba, goods were loaded for Sint Maarten, and via the Dominican Republic, where food from the World Food Programme was taken on board for Dominica, the vessel again set course for Sint Maarten and Dominica. In Sint Maarten, aid supplies were unloaded again, and a RIP was conducted with Zr.Ms. Zeeland. Additionally, children from the local Oranjeschool were given a tour of the ship. After departing from Sint Maarten, the ship set course for Martinique to pick up emergency aid for Dominica. On the latter island, emergency aid was unloaded again. To make room at the quay, the ship quickly departed again to sea. Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman carried out the redeployment for the entire task force present in Sint Maarten. The onload was a significant task for which a new loading plan was developed.
