During this exercise, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter worked closely with NATO allies and partners, enhancing interoperability and joint operational capabilities. After returning to Den Helder on 19 June, the ship underwent maintenance and crew training until the end of July. 

On 1 August, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter set sail again, this time for a deployment to the Caribbean as part of the Dutch Caribbean Coast Guard efforts. The ship conducted various patrols and provided support during the hurricane season, including humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations. 

On 30 September, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter returned to Den Helder, where the crew was welcomed back by family and friends. The year concluded with a series of internal evaluations and preparations for the upcoming year, ensuring that the ship and crew were ready for future missions and challenges.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.24)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-24 99 The Operations Directorate training period was conducted under the direction of the Dutch STC. Subsequently, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter participated as an air defense unit and fighter controller in the NATO Tiger Meet exercise off the west coast of France. After returning to her home port on June 15, the ship prepared for the Marine Days combined with SAIL Den Helder from June 22 to June 25. During this event, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter served as the flagship in the harbor of Den Helder during the SAIL Out of the tall ships, with onboard C-ZSK, the SAIL organization, and approximately 250 invited guests. Shortly after the summer leave, the ship was designated to escort, among others, two Russian submarines through the Dutch EEZ. Following this, the ship and her crew prepared from September 19 for participation in the Joint Warrior 17-2 exercise. During this exercise, the vessel also participated in the American-led ballistic missile defense exercise Formidable Shield 17. In this context, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter, together with external technicians, succeeded in tracking a ballistic test missile in space with her modified SMART-L radar. The missile was subsequently successfully engaged by an American unit. After returning to Den Helder on October 18, a subsequent sailing period commenced on November 28, primarily to support the sailing practice for navigation officers in training. On December 15, the ship returned to Den Helder. Zr.Ms. De Ruyter during SAIL in Den Helder.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.25)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-25 100 Operations Directorate Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) E.C.W. Jansen In 2017, Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën was undergoing multi-year maintenance. Zr.Ms. Evertsen Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) W.H. van Gemeren The year 2017 started off intensively for Zr.Ms. Evertsen: After a stormy Staff Sea Check, the ship and her crew were prepared from January 16 to 27 as part of the SARC4 for the upcoming Netherlands Operational Sea Training (NOST) period. On February 11, Zr.Ms. Evertsen entered the port of Plymouth and commenced the NOST. It was a very educational period in which the crew of Zr.Ms. Evertsen was elevated to a higher level in all aspects. The hard work and enthusiastic commitment of the crew were ultimately rewarded on March 24 with a very rare "Good on the final inspection" and "Overall very satisfactory," after which the Commander STC CZSK declared the ship operationally deployable. Earlier in the NOST, Zr.Ms. Evertsen had also set a 'record' with the FOST training of the crew on Zr.Ms. Evertsen.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.26)
sections.text: Directie Operaties when it fulfilled the role of CTG over no less than 16 operational units during the largest weekly war in recent NOST history. The remainder of 2017 was marked for Zr.Ms. Evertsen by participation in SNMG1. After a very successful family day on May 4, the ship departed for the Baltic Sea to join the NATO fleet under the command of Norwegian Commander O. M. Sandqvist. The fleet operated in the Baltic Sea as part of the so-called 'reassurance measures' from NATO for the countries in the region. In its first week in the area, Zr.Ms. Evertsen made the news after two Russian Su-24 Fencer fighter jets flew relatively low past the ship three times. The incident posed no threat, but the activities of the aircraft were closely monitored. With SNMG1, Zr.Ms. Evertsen also participated in the large NATO exercise BALTOPS17 and undertook several port visits in the region. Before the fleet departed towards the coast of Iceland for participation in the major NATO submarine warfare exercise Dynamic Mongoose17, a port visit was made to Kiel during the famous Kieler Woche. Before and after Dynamic Mongoose17, Reykjavik was visited. On July 12, Zr.Ms. Evertsen returned to the port of Den Helder and, after a maintenance week, could commence summer leave. On September 4, the ship went back to sea and rejoined SNMG1 after passing through the Kiel Canal (which part of the crew cycled through). After participating in the first phase of the NATO exercise: Northern Coasts, the fleet headed towards the Mediterranean Sea and passed through the Strait of Gibraltar on September 23. During its stay in the Mediterranean Sea, Zr.Ms. Evertsen was part of Operation Sea Guardian, aimed at monitoring suspicious air and maritime traffic in the region. This operation replaces the former Article 5 operation ACTIVE ENDEAVOUR. The ship first made a port visit in southern France in Toulon, before participating in the next NATO exercise Brilliant Mariner17. After its successful completion, in which Zr.Ms. Evertsen played an important role as the 'missile umbrella' of the group, the NATO fleet set course for Algiers. This port visit was part of the Mediterranean Dialogue, a program with seven non-NATO countries including Algeria. This aims to contribute to stability and security in the region. During the port visit, free passage was not allowed, but thanks to several organized excursions, a large part of the crew still got some

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.27)
sections.text: 102 Operations Directorate image of the North African city. There were also a number of lucky individuals who won a lunch at the residence of the Dutch ambassador through a charity auction. On October 16, a sail past was held to bid farewell to the NATO naval group, and Zr.Ms. Evertsen set course for Den Helder, where a maintenance period began on October 20. The remaining weeks of 2017 were spent in home port. Zr.Ms. Tromp Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) K. Schipper After a short leave following Operation Atalanta, the year for Zr.Ms. Tromp began with preparations for exercise TG 17-1 under the leadership of the Norwegian Navy. The priority for this exercise was to support and execute the Eyes Only portion of the SMCC of the Dutch, Norwegian, and British submarine services. Zr.Ms. Tromp also supported the training for navigation officer Groot Bovenwater, alongside Zr.Ms. Groningen. After this deployment, there was a short period in port, after which Zr.Ms. Tromp participated for the second consecutive year in the spring edition of exercise Joint Warrior. The ship acted as the flagship for the Multi-National Forces, the armed forces tasked with re-stabilizing a conflict area from the sea. To this end, the Hebrides, islands off the northwest coast of Scotland, were transformed into an area torn apart by war and years of division. Together with Zr.Ms. De Ruyter and USS Carney, and other units, a week of combat was conducted against the Dragonian forces, simulated by the NATO task group SNMG1. Under the leadership of Commander (cdr) C.H. Boelema Robertus, the Multi-National Forces succeeded in guaranteeing peace and security from the sea. Parallel to exercise Joint Warrior, the second part of the SMCC took place, where the program was entirely focused on safely operating a submarine under tactical conditions. Both Zr.Ms. De Ruyter and Zr.Ms. Tromp served as opposition for Zr.Ms. Bruinvis and a Norwegian submarine. Not only the aspiring commanders but also the anti-submarine warfare team of Zr.Ms. Tromp gained valuable operational experience during these exercises. After three busy weeks, a very welcome but short port visit to Dublin followed. After

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.28)
sections.text: Directie Operations Zr.Ms. Tromp in the port of Den Helder.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.29)
sections.text: Directie Operaties departed on Monday, setting course for the FOST areas south of Great Britain; familiar territory for many. For three days, Zr.Ms. Tromp participated in an intensive training program under the guidance of FOST; given the numerous crew changes (approximately 60%), this was certainly no luxury. After the Weekly War concluded on Thursday afternoon, the ship returned to Den Helder. The intensive spring was followed by a quiet period of several months in port. However, the crew of Zr.Ms. Tromp did not remain idle. In total, the ship conducted eight sailing days in 2017 for Recruitment & Selection and the Communication department of CZSK and also participated in the Marine Days in Den Helder. On June 8, Zr.Ms. Tromp sailed for a demonstration of Replenishment at Sea with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman for a working visit from the outgoing Minister of Defence J.A. Hennis-Plasschaert. Most of the time was spent on Assisted Maintenance, during which the Technical Service and the involved shore authorities made significant efforts to prepare the ship for the autumn voyage. This autumn voyage kicked off in Rotterdam with the World Port Days, where Zr.Ms. Tromp, together with other units and civilian parties, welcomed approximately 430,000 visitors during the first weekend of September. Following the World Port Days, the ship, along with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel, and BNS Louise-Marie, steamed towards the Baltic Sea. This task group would participate over a period of seven weeks in three major international exercises: Northern Coasts, Joint Warrior 17-2, and Formidable Shield 2017. The staff of the task group, this time under the command of Commander (cdr) J.H. Hulsker, was once again embarked on Zr.Ms. Tromp. After a weekend in Karlskrona, Northern Coasts commenced. This exercise focused on international cooperation in the Baltic Sea, with the secondary goal of the SARC-4 of Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman. However, this was withdrawn halfway through the exercise for humanitarian assistance in the Caribbean following Hurricane Irma. After a weekend of relaxation in Oslo, the group steamed further towards the seas around Scotland. While the scenario of Joint Warrior was already familiar to the crew, participation in Formidable Shield was new for many of the crew members. Zr.Ms. Tromp, together with Zr.Ms. De Ruyter, provided the Dutch contribution to this MISSILEX. Formidable Shield was led by the Americans and focused on Ballistic Missile Defense and Integrated Air Missile Defense. Although the weather was unfavorable due to the passing Hurricane Ophelia, all scenarios in which the Netherlands participated were able to take place. During two of these events, the ship successfully launched one SM-2 and three ESSM.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.30)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-30 105 The Operations Directorate was launched. One of these scenarios involved a high incoming supersonic target, a first for the Dutch fire control chain. At the end of October, Zr.Ms. Tromp was back in Den Helder. The last voyage of 2017 was a short trip of two weeks with a lot of variety. The first three days were focused on the training of the navigation officer for large surface vessels. Together with Zr.Ms. De Ruyter and the units of SNMG1, there was intensive maneuvering and navigation for three days. After three days, the trainees transferred to Zr.Ms. De Ruyter, after which Zr.Ms. Tromp could begin the transit to Copenhagen. After a good weekend in this beautiful harbor, the ship conducted several days of helicopter qualification for the pilot training, before mooring for the last time of the year in Den Helder on Friday, December 15. Zr.Ms. Van Amstel Commanding Officer: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) H.J.F. Toebast, from August 29 Lieutenant Commander (kltz) P.J. Hol The year 2017 began for Zr.Ms. Van Amstel with an Assisted Maintenance period in preparation for the voyage to the Caribbean in the spring. In addition to maintenance, under the leadership of Departure Zr.Ms. Van Amstel to the mission area was carried out.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.31)
sections.text: The Operations Directorate (Directie Operaties) conducted a three-day Pre Deployment Training in week 6. On February 17, there was a Home Front Information Day, and on February 21 and 22, the Law Enforcement Detachment (LEDET) of the US Coast Guard (USCG) visited the ship and made the necessary preparations for the period as (SSCG) until March 4. On March 4, the day of departure, a large part of the crew was awarded the Humanitarian Assistance Medal for Disaster Relief in the presence of family and friends due to their efforts in the Mediterranean in the spring of 2016 (FRONTEX). The transit to Curaçao began with a severe storm over the Bay of Biscay. As a result, the embarked NH90 was forced to disembark and eventually returned on board from Spain after the storm had passed. The crossing of the Atlantic Ocean focused on the exercise and training of the crew, with an emphasis on training the Ship Boarding Team, culminating in a final exercise near Sint Maarten where a boarding was conducted on a cutter of the Caribbean Coast Guard. During the transit from Sint Maarten to Curaçao, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel conducted a Replenishment at Sea (RAS) with RFA Wave Knight on March 16. On March 17, the ship ceremonially entered the port of Willemstad. At the staff hill of CZMCARIB, the ship's staff was prepared for the upcoming period with the arrival of the station ship Zr.Ms. Van Amstel in Curaçao.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.32)
sections.text: 107 Operations Directorate various briefings, after which the ship went back to sea on March 20 to perform coast guard duties near the ABC islands. During this period, the ship conducted routine checks, carried out helicopter patrols, and during Operation Lockdown, monitored the incoming and outgoing shipping traffic of Willemstad. On March 24, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel towed a disabled fishing vessel, the 'Vicamar', to Kralendijk. On April 4, the ship conducted a DISTEX at the Marine Barracks Savaneta in Aruba, and the next day it ceremonially entered the port of Oranjestad. There, the USCG LEDET was embarked. After departing from Oranjestad on April 9, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel began its CTG 4.4 period. On April 11, the ship conducted a Naval Surface Fire Support exercise with the 76 mm gun north of Aruba. During the CTG 4.4 period, the ship managed to intercept several Go-Fast vessels and seize contraband. In total, this amounted to 1356 kg of drugs and 4000 liters of fuel. The contraband and the crew members of the Go-Fasts were handed over to the USCG. During this period, a port visit to Cartagena also took place, and helicopter fuel (F44) was loaded in Colon, Panama. The CTG 4.4 period was interrupted by a period at the Atlantic Undersea Test and Evaluation Centre (AUTEC) range, preceded by a port visit to Mayport. At the AUTEC range, the ship, together with USS Forrest Sherman and USS Jason Dunham, conducted various anti-submarine warfare exercises, with Zr.Ms. Van Amstel focusing on testing the LFAPS system (towed sonar). The AUTEC period concluded with a port visit to Key West. After this, the CTG 4.4 period was to be continued, had it not been for problems with the drinking water supply on board that caused delays. Instead of patrolling, the ship went on main routes to Curaçao to repair the drinking water system during an eight-day port visit. The ship then returned to the Netherlands, where the crew was welcomed by family and friends in Den Helder on June 16. After a week of compensatory leave, there was time for necessary maintenance until the start of the summer leave on July 22. The week before the leave, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel escorted a Chinese squadron as RDS from July 16 to 18, and on July 19, there was a sailing family day. Immediately after the summer leave, on August 29, Lieutenant Commander (kltz) P.J. Hol took command of Zr.Ms. Van Amstel from Lieutenant Commander (kltz) H.J.F. Toebast. The following week, the ship began a five-week journey with the transit (under the command of NLMARFOR) to Karlskrona, during which an NH90 was embarked and a BOZ.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.33)
sections.text:
operations of Zr.Ms. Van Speijk out of various patrols and exercises in the Caribbean region. The ship conducted maritime security operations and participated in joint exercises with local authorities. The crew also engaged in community outreach activities, strengthening ties with the local population. 

Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman Commander: kltz J. de Vries The operations of the Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman were executed successfully. After Karlskrona, the Northern Coasts exercise commenced, during which various exercises took place together with forty ships from multiple countries. For Zr.Ms. Van Amstel, the focus was on anti-submarine warfare. Both the ship and the NH90 launched practice torpedoes during this exercise. After a port visit to Oslo, the frigate conducted degaussing in Wilhelmshaven on September 27 before continuing to Kristiansand. After this port, measurements were taken on the noise measurement track in Heggernes on October 3 and 4, with a return to Den Helder on October 6. Week 41 was a busy week for the Technical Service, during which extensive maintenance was carried out to prepare for sailing the following week. From October 16 to 20, a Helicopter Qualification (HQ) week was conducted, followed by a week of compensatory leave. After a period of technical issues, the ship sailed from November 15 to 17 to determine new Ship Helicopter Operating Limits (SHOL) for the NH90. The planned ACT-ASW trip did not take place due to a defective LFAPS system. In week 50, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel sailed for NATO training. The two aspiring navigation officers on board both passed their assessments. After returning, the ship was prepared for end-of-year leave. 

Zr.Ms. Van Speijk Commander: kltz R. van Twuijver With a crew of 160, the new station ship Zr.Ms. Van Speijk entered the Annabaai of Curaçao for the first time on November 10. Unlike its predecessor, this period a multipurpose frigate carries out the tasks of the station ship. Its arrival was accompanied by the usual ceremonial events, saluting shots, and honors to the Governor of Curaçao. The first port visit of Zr.Ms. Van Speijk to Aruba also included such ceremonies. Together with the coast guard, the ship rescued nine castaways. The DASH-8 patrol aircraft from the Caribbean Coast Guard discovered the distressed vessel. Zr.Ms. Van Speijk was nearby when the crew of the ship indicated that it was taking on water and sinking. Shortly thereafter, a fire broke out, and it was reported over the radio that the ship was unmanageable. The nine crew members (6 Venezuelans, 2 Colombians, and 1 Dominican) then jumped overboard. With the NH90 onboard helicopter and the small vessels from Van Speijk, the castaways were retrieved from the water, taken aboard Zr.Ms. Van Speijk, and provided with care. Furthermore, the operations of Zr.Ms. Van Speijk included various patrols and exercises in the Caribbean region. The ship conducted maritime security operations and participated in joint exercises with local authorities. The crew also engaged in community outreach activities, strengthening ties with the local population.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.34)
sections.text: Directorate Operations coast guard periods from patrols near the Windward and Leeward Islands. During this time, there were periods of lockdown, and the SABES and Vista del Condor operations were carried out. The ship also conducted successful drug interdiction operations. In the first drug case, approximately 550 kilograms of cocaine was intercepted. This occurred during the night of December 21 to 22. The second case began on Christmas Day. An initial search did not yield the desired results, after which permission was requested to conduct a thorough search of the suspicious vessel while still in the Dominican Republic. In consultation with the Dominican authorities, it was decided to bring the ship into Santo Domingo for a dockside boarding. Here, the case was handed over to the Dominican Republic, and 1600 kilograms of cocaine was found. Zr.Ms. Friesland Commander: Lieutenant (ltz) 1 H. van den Berg (acting), from May 11 Lieutenant Commander (kltz) N.I.J. Kuipers EMSD The year 2017 was marked for Zr.Ms. Friesland by its first scheduled maintenance and subsequently the reactivation of the ship and crew to become operational again. Zr.Ms. Van Speijk during an exercise in the North Sea.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.35)
sections.text: The Operations Directorate. At the beginning of the year, the ship was moored at the docks at the DMI for the scheduled maintenance. A significant portion of the maintenance took place in the dry dock in Den Helder from February through April. The first milestone in the process of making the ship operational was the appointment of the new commander, Captain (ktz) N.I.J. Kuipers EMSD, on May 11. She took command from the acting commander, Lieutenant Commander (kltz) 1 H. van den Berg. After the summer leave, the focus of maintenance shifted to the training period, so that the ship would achieve operational readiness status in 2018. The crew worked hard during this period to be able to sail safely as a unit. After an intensive and varied training period, Zr.Ms. Friesland departed for sea on October 2 for the SARC-3, as the first sailing unit of the training trajectory. The SARC-3 was an intensive period for the ship, especially since a lot of time was spent on command transfer on Zr.Ms. Friesland during the preparations.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.36)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-36 111 Directorate Operations the completion of the maintenance was allocated. As a result, two additional sailing days were made on October 19 and 20, after which the vessel received the designation 'seaworthy' from CSTC. Following this milestone, Zr.Ms. Friesland received the notification that the water mist system had been disapproved, resulting in the withdrawal of the ship's seaworthiness certificate. Due to this setback, the ship remained alongside for the rest of 2017, which meant that the planned sailing material tests, including the first foreign port visit and SARC-4 in 2017, did not take place. Zr.Ms. Groningen Commander: kltz H.M. Sinke The year began for Zr.Ms. Groningen with a maintenance period and SAT of the Main Propulsion Diesel Engines (HVD). In mid-January, the ship departed to sea to serve as a sparring partner during the SARC-4 of Zr.Ms. Evertsen. This exercise period was conducted in the FOST areas near Plymouth. After a port visit to Southampton, as part of training and international cooperation, a Dutch NH 90 helicopter with a mixed Dutch and Belgian crew landed on Zr.Ms. Zeeland.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.37)
sections.text: The Operations Directorate received the order to escort a Russian task force, including the aircraft carrier RFS Admiral Kuznetsov, through the North Sea. Zr.Ms. Groningen conducted a Replenishment at Sea (RAS) with the German tanker FGS Spessart while escorting this task force. At the beginning of February, the ship departed again for sea to support the SMCC and the practical part of the navigation officer training, the NATO sailing practice. Zr.Ms. Groningen first exercised with NLMARSOF during the outbound journey. The SMCC took place on Zr.Ms. Walrus in the Norwegian fjords, and therefore the ship made two brief visits to the port of Bergen. In March, Zr.Ms. Groningen conducted helicopter qualifications and received the Inspector General of the Armed Forces, Lieutenant General H. van Griensven. The ship visited Delfzijl to maintain the relationship with its namesake, the province of Groningen. During a reception, the mayor was welcomed. The ship also held an 'open house,' where around 1,000 residents of Groningen admired the vessel. Upon returning to Den Helder, the ship organized a sailing family day. In April, Zr.Ms. Groningen sailed for several days for Communications CZSK and for DCPL to inspire interested parties about the sailing operations. The ship's godmother, former Minister Melanie Schultz van Haegen, also sailed along. As a sparring partner during Zr.Ms. Holland at SAIL in Den Helder, it was positioned behind the Russian four-masted barque Krusenstern.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.38)
sections.text: The Operations Directorate SARC-4 of Zr.Ms. Zeeland made a brief port visit to Aarhus. There, a delegation from the Dutch school visited the ship, during which lessons were conducted on board. After returning to Den Helder, Zr.Ms. Groningen began preparatory work for the Scheduled Maintenance. From the end of April, the ship was in the so-called T-status. At the end of September, Zr.Ms. Groningen was cold-moved to the Rijkswerf, where maintenance began. From November 24, the ship was in the dock at the Rijkswerf. Zr.Ms. Holland Commander: kltz P.C.B. Dijkhuizen EMSD The deployment of Zr.Ms. Holland this year consisted of three parts: a training program led by C-STC, Coast Guard duties, and counter-drug operations. After the maintenance period in Curaçao, Zr.Ms. Holland conducted CD operations from December 13, 2016, to January 20, 2017, with support from the USCG LEDET and a Guard Aviation Detachment with an MH-65 Dolphin helicopter. After completing a joint training/integration period, the ship was ready for Operation Carib Venture under the leadership of CTG 4.4. During this period, two drug transports were disrupted, and the ship was closely involved in a controlled overload of contraband. During the Coast Guard operation periods, daily FRISC patrols were again conducted around the Windward Islands and in the waters around Anguilla and Saint Kitts. On January 21, in close cooperation with the DASH-8, an interception of a Go-Fast was carried out, resulting in the seizure of 220 kg of cocaine and the arrest of three individuals by the Coast Guard boarding team. Zr.Ms. Holland transferred the vessel, the contraband, and the suspects to the public prosecutor in Sint Maarten. On the last patrol day, the ship intercepted a suspicious vessel that was landing on Bonaire with narcotics, a firearm, and two individuals. Zr.Ms. Holland also assisted a British sailing yacht that was experiencing hydraulic problems with its steering system. The technical personnel of Zr.Ms. Holland repaired the installation, allowing the sailing yacht to continue its journey to Bonaire under its own power.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.39)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-39 114 Operations Directorate In addition to various SAR actions, the successful disruption of several drug transports, and two actual drug seizures totaling 284.5 kg of cocaine, the ship also visited several ports. Zr.Ms. Zeeland Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) A. van der Kamp Zr.Ms. Zeeland departed from the port of Den Helder during the Marine Days to make the crossing to the Caribbean. During the outbound journey, a fire broke out on the port side HVD. Due to prompt action with handheld fire extinguishers, the damage was limited, and the journey could continue with a functioning HVD. During the crossing, the ship's boarding team was trained by the Boarding Operations Bureau. Due to excessive fuel consumption, the ship had to make an unscheduled port visit to Ponta Delgada in Madeira. During the crossing, the second HVD failed, causing the ship to make the crossing using only two patrol electric motors (PEM) at a maximum speed of 8 knots. After 13 days on the PEMs, Zr.Ms. Zeeland and her crew reached Curaçao on July 12. On September 4, Zr.Ms. Zeeland received the order to provide emergency assistance following the passage of Hurricane Irma. The ship sailed via Aruba, where emergency relief supplies and personnel were taken on board. The exercise of the abandonment role of Zr.Ms. Zeeland in Den Helder via a liferaft.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.40)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-40 115 The Operations Directorate embarked and sailed to the Windward Islands of the Kingdom. Zr.Ms. Zeeland provided support to the Commander of the 'emergency aid' detachment, later renamed Commander Joint Task Force Sint-Maarten. The priorities were to support security and transport tasks, assess the damage, and operationalize the infrastructure (including the air and seaport). Four days after Hurricane Irma passed, a second hurricane announced itself in the region: José. As a result, both Zr.Ms. Zeeland and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan (which was also in Sint-Maarten for emergency aid) had to leave the port to seek shelter at a safe distance. Fortunately, the damage from Hurricane José was limited. On September 19, a third hurricane approached: Maria. After tearing across Dominica, Maria veered towards Puerto Rico, sparing the Dutch Windward Islands from further disaster. As the emergency aid in Sint-Maarten transitioned to a reconstruction phase, Zr.Ms. Zeeland, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman, and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan provided emergency aid to Dominica. Distributing essential supplies to isolated areas and conducting medical evacuations were the tasks of these naval vessels. In total, Zeeland and her crew operated for 36 consecutive days at sea and on land as part of emergency aid operations. Due to the emergency aid operations, Zr.Ms. Zeeland could be deployed more restrictively for coast guard tasks. Nevertheless, the ship managed to rescue a 60-year-old sailor from Saint Vincent from the water during her coast guard periods and participated in Operation Lockdown Aruba. On the first night of Zr.Ms. Zeeland's return journey, the Coast Guard's DASH-8 aircraft spotted a suspicious boat. Both the NH90 helicopter and the two FRISC boats were deployed to intercept the vessel. After it ignored warning shots, disabling fire was used to disable the outboard motors. The occupants of the boat threw suspicious packages overboard. With the FRISC, 348 kilograms of cocaine were retrieved from the water. Minehunter Zr.Ms. Makkum Commander: Lt. Cdr. B.R.P. Clasen The operational year for Zr.Ms. Makkum began with the execution of SARC-4 in February, during which the British port of Leith was the first foreign port of the year visited. However, during this work-up period, a problem arose with the port side rudder stock.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.41)
sections.text:
the maintenance period on leave. On 1 July, Zr.Ms. Schiedam set sail for the Baltic Sea to participate in the exercise BALTOPS 17. During this exercise, which lasted until 18 June, the ship conducted various operations, including anti-submarine warfare, air defense, and maritime security operations. The ship returned to Den Helder on 20 June, where it underwent a short maintenance period before preparing for the next deployment. 

On 1 August, Zr.Ms. Schiedam departed for a mission in the Caribbean as part of the Caribbean Task Force. The ship arrived in Willemstad, Curaçao, on 5 August, where it conducted various tasks, including maritime surveillance and support for local authorities in combating drug trafficking. The ship also participated in community engagement activities, strengthening ties with the local population. 

Zr.Ms. Schiedam returned to Den Helder on 15 October, concluding its Caribbean deployment. After a brief maintenance period, the ship prepared for the winter exercises and the upcoming operational year. The year ended with a successful completion of all planned missions and exercises, demonstrating the ship's capabilities and the professionalism of its crew.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.42)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-42 117 Operations Directorate during this period spread across various units and departments. In week 27, the ship returned to Den Helder to then sail for two more weeks under the banner of Beneficial Cooperation (BC), during which various explosives were searched for on the seabed. After the summer leave, the ship participated from week 36 to week 39 in the exercise Northern Coasts, where, among other things, mine hunting was practiced under an increased threat. The ship also conducted a BOZ exercise with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman as the first minehunter. After NOCO, the ship sailed for several more BC weeks in combination with the tasks of RDS, culminating in a visit to Schiedam. During this visit, several guests were embarked near Hoek van Holland to sail together to the 'home port' Schiedam. The group of embarkees consisted of invitees from the Schiedam distillery De Ruyter and prize winners from Schiedam and the surrounding area. After this successful visit, the ship sailed for the last time that year to Zeebrugge for maintenance. Zr.Ms. Urk Commander: Lt. G.E. Fretz In mid-January, the ship was taken to Zeebrugge for major maintenance. Subsequently, a training period began, during which crew members attended courses, completed tests, and made preparations. In early March, part of the crew boarded Zr.Ms. Urk in Zeebrugge. They ensured that the ship completed SARC 1, after which the rest of the crew embarked to complete SARC-2. Furthermore, Lieutenant (ltz) G.E. Fretz took command. In May, SARC-3 was scheduled for two weeks. Despite many material defects, the status Ready for Sea was achieved. Before the leave, several SATs were conducted, and a signature measurement took place on the Haringvliet. After the summer leave, the crew began the second half of the training trajectory. In August, the ship worked on an exercise program in Zeebrugge as part of SARC-4, during which a lot of diving took place. After successfully completing this week, Zr.Ms. Urk set course for Scotland for two weeks of exercises in the Firth of Forth.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.43)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-43 118 Operations Directorate near Edinburgh. Here, mine hunting was practiced intensively, and due to the deeper waters around Scotland, the Self Propelled Variable Depth Sonar (SPVDS) was well utilized. As a break from the training program, a weekend stop was made in Leith near Edinburgh. Upon arrival in Zeebrugge, it became clear that we had successfully completed SARC-4 and that Zr.Ms. Urk received the designation Ready for Exercise. In October, the final phase of the training trajectory began. SARC-5 consisted of four weeks filled with scheduled exercises in firefighting, mine hunting, force protection, and multiple emergencies. This was good preparation for SARC-6, which immediately followed SARC-5. During this week, various exercises were conducted, but this time the exercises were unexpectedly initiated by the MOST. Despite a good start to SARC-5/6 and the enthusiastic commitment of the crew, this period unfortunately concluded with an unsatisfactory result, meaning that Zr.Ms. Urk will conduct SARC-5/6 again in March 2018. After these intensive weeks, an annual maintenance (JO) period immediately began, during which a large portion of the crew was assigned to various placements. Furthermore, in the last week of the year, the ship was taken to dry dock at Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen in the port of Den Helder.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.44)
sections.text: ces van de oefening. Op 2 juli 2017 arriveerde Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen in de Baltische Zee en nam deel aan de oefening US BALTOPS. Gedurende deze oefening werden diverse scenario's geoefend, waaronder het uitvoeren van mijnenbestrijdingsoperaties en samenwerking met andere marines. Na afloop van de oefening keerde het schip terug naar Zeebrugge voor de laatste onderhoudswerkzaamheden. In augustus 2017 werd Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen opnieuw ingezet voor een aantal BC weken, waarbij het schip verschillende contacten heeft gelokaliseerd en geruimd. De inzet van Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen in 2017 heeft bijgedragen aan de versterking van de samenwerking met andere marines en de lokale gemeenschap.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.45)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-45 120 The Operations Directorate designated minehunters for the approach to Swinoujscie, Poland. From here, BALTOPS was initiated, which took place near the island of Bornholm. Among other activities, minehunting exercises, maneuvering exercises, and simulated air attacks were conducted. Surface target shooting was also carried out for the exercise. The period concluded with a visit to Kieler Woche, after which the ship sailed back through the Kiel Canal to Den Helder for SAIL Den Helder. During these days, the ship was open to visitors. After embarking a new group of cadets, the task group at sea was chosen, and after various exercises with the group, SAIL Wilhelmshaven was visited. Upon departure, Commander (Cdr) J.H. Hulsker came on board. The commander was given a tour of the ship, focusing on the (weapon) technical spaces. The next port visit was Stavanger, including a beautiful navigation exercise towards the famous cliff Preikestolen. Due to the misty conditions and the natural beauty, this was a very impressive journey. After various fire, towing, and BOZ exercises in the North Sea, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen returned to her home port of Den Helder in mid-July. In the autumn, BC tasks were again carried out, followed by a maintenance period in Zeebrugge. The ship also went to the Haringvliet for a week to reassess the magnetic and acoustic signature. Zr.Ms. Willemstad Commanding Officer: Lieutenant (ltz1) Y.A. van Beusekom 2017 was an active year for Zr.Ms. Willemstad, during which she participated in various exercises. Although several technical problems arose throughout the year, Willemstad and her crew dedicated themselves to training and education, displaying the Dutch flag, and promoting the Royal Netherlands Navy in general. After completing the annual maintenance in Zeebrugge, the year for Zr.Ms. Willemstad began in March with participation in the international exercise Joint Warrior near Scotland. In the spring, the ship contributed to testing future mine countermeasure equipment in cooperation with the Belgian Navy. After this, she represented the Dutch Navy during SAIL Den Helder and Marine Days in Den Helder, where approximately 1,500 people were guided on board. Willemstad also participated in July in the Cadet Cruise, focusing on training six future officers. After taking part in

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.46)
sections.text: The Operations Directorate participated in the World Port Days in Rotterdam in August, where an estimated 2000 people were on board. In September, there was participation in the international exercise Northern Coasts in the Baltic Sea. After this, the minehunter returned to Zeebrugge to be prepared for the Scheduled Maintenance. Zr.Ms. Zierikzee Commander: Lieutenant (ltz1) J.A.G. Egberts The ship was under maintenance for the entire year. Submarine Service Zr.Ms. Bruinvis Commander: Lieutenant (ltz1) M.F. Mertens No contribution was received. The new simulator of the Submarine Service in action in Den Helder.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.47)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-47 122 Operations Directorate Zr.Ms. Dolfijn In 2017, the submarine was under maintenance. Zr.Ms. Walrus Commander: Lt Commander (ltz1) B.A. van de Kraats, from May 19 Lt Commander (ltz1) J.W. Vroegop Zr.Ms. Walrus made three voyages during the year 2017. From January 30 to February 17, the voyage took place in which the submarine facilitated the Commanding Officers Course Qualifying Exercise (COCQEX) in Norwegian waters for both the NLSMCC and the British SMCC. During this voyage, students were tested in safely operating a submarine at periscope depth among warships maneuvering at high speed around the submarine. During this voyage, a port visit to Bergen took place. Zr.Ms. Walrus in British waters.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.48)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-48 123 Operations Directorate Once back in Den Helder, Zr.Ms. Walrus entered dry dock for Periodic Docking number 4, with the aim of being made ready for deployment for a CDS operation later in the year. This period was also used to carry out a crew change. Crew Orange, previously working on Zr.Ms. Bruinvis, exchanged with Crew Blue, who were working on Zr.Ms. Walrus. Crew Orange would later carry out the CDS operation with the Walrus later in the year following this exchange. After the crew change and maintenance period, trials after maintenance, Combat Training (CT), and a Pre Deployment Training took place in preparation for the CDS operation. The Walrus had to carry out the BNO program intermittently due to several significant malfunctions that required a return to Den Helder. After completing the trials, Zr.Ms. Walrus successfully executed the CDS operation. From November 19 to December 2, the third voyage took place, focusing on Zr.Ms. Mercuur near Plymouth.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.49)
sections.text: 124 Operations Directorate provided support to FOST and 7 SQN. In addition, there was a focus on training our own personnel. The program during these two weeks mainly consisted of CASEX B2 with air units and several CASEX A24 with surface and air units. The NH90s from 7 SQN participated in the serials at various times. Additionally, Zr.Ms. Walrus advanced crew members with an INDEX program in their training trajectory. Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw Commander: Lt. Cdr. E.G.J. Ruijsink No contributions received. Zr.Ms. Mercuur Commander: Lt. Cdr. R.H.G. Woertman For the first time in over two years, Zr.Ms. Mercuur sailed from Den Helder towards the Baltic Sea with the aim of facilitating the Adelborsten Cruise. After several port visits, the ship returned to its home port on July 14. After the summer leave, Mercuur was in service for the training program of Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw. On November 15, both ships jointly docked again in Den Helder. Operational units Marine Corps 1st Marine Combat Group (1 MCG) Commander: Lt. Col. I.D.L. Moerman, from September 1 Lt. Col. E. Piwek The first half of 2017 was largely focused on supporting the training of 13 Raiding Squadron (RSQN) and 22 RSQN. In the first quarter, the Joint Arctic Training 2017 (JAT17) demanded all attention. 12 RSQN began its training program in August. After the summer leave of 2017, the training of the MCG staff commenced.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.50)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-50 125 Operations Directorate Individual Deployments Various personnel from 1 MCG participated in individual deployments in 2017, including the Capacity Building Mission Iraq (CBMI, both regular and Special Operations Forces (SOF)). Very High Readiness Joint Task Force (Land) (VJTF(L)) The VJTF(L) is a rapidly deployable brigade and is under British command. The Netherlands contributed a Raiding Squadron Task Unit (RSTU) in 2017, consisting of approximately 180 personnel. The main body was formed by 1 RSQN, supplemented by enablers from 10 Combat Service Support Squadron (10 CSS SQN), 14 Combat Support Squadron (14 CS SQN), and 15 Reconnaissance Target Acquisition Squadron (15 RSTA SQN). From January 1 to December 31, 2017, the entire VJTF(L) was on 48 hours notice to move for deployment within NATO territory. Marine Spearhead Task Unit (MSTU) The MSTU is a rapidly deployable unit of the Marine Corps that can be deployed within 48 hours. The core of the unit is a Raiding Squadron, supplemented with enablers in Sint Maarten after Hurricane Irma.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.51)
sections.text: Operations Directorate of Combat Service Support Squadron, Combat Support Squadron, and Reconnaissance Target Acquisition Squadron. Command & control is provided by a staff element of the MCG staff. In 2017, this task was assigned to 1 MCG. FPME-4 From July 18, a composite unit from 1 MCG participated for three months in the Force Protection Middle East (FPME) mission number 4 in Jordan. The unit was responsible for providing security for a Belgian squadron of F-16s. The CLSK was unable to execute rotation 4 due to the fact that the appropriate security personnel were on deployment protection. Not providing Force Protection was not an option because the Netherlands had an agreement with Belgium that if they supplied the F-16s, the Netherlands would provide ground security. Colleagues from the CLSK were also added to the security detachment of 1 MCG. During the mission, there was excellent cooperation. Emergency Assistance Sint Maarten 11 Raiding Squadron (including the reinforcement of a Troop from 23 Raiding Squadron), BME, and logistics personnel from 1 MCG provided emergency assistance in Sint Maarten following Hurricane Irma from September 8 to the end of September. In addition, 1 MCG supplied the majority of the staff officers, together with personnel from 2 MCG, to form the command and control element of the Joint Task Force Sint Maarten. VPD (Vessel Protection Detachment) As in previous years, VPD teams were also deployed in 2017 to secure Dutch ships. This year, 2 MCG provided the six primary VPD teams and 1 MCG was required to provide five secondary VPD teams. This led to several deployments. National Assistance Personnel from 1 MCG also saw deployment in the national domain in 2017. For example, from August 12 to August 20, a Maritime Advanced Search Team (MAST) provided support for an operation in Curaçao. Atalanta 2017 From August 27 to December 3, personnel from Recce Sniper, supplemented by personnel from 22 RSQN, participated as EBE in the Atalanta mission aboard Zr.Ms. Rotterdam as part of the European Union's anti-piracy mission.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.52)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-52 127 Operations Directorate Training and Exercises The larger exercises of 2017 included the JAT in the vicinity of Harstad (Norway), the Black Horse shooting training at Twentynine Palms (United States), and the mountain training in Garelochhead (United Kingdom). 10 CSS SQN was on 48 hours notice to move for the VJTF in 2017 with approximately half of the squadron, personnel as well as equipment. The squadron had logistical resources ready for 30 days to enable an expeditionary operation, entirely independently. At the same time, the squadron supported the other exercises of 1 MCG, in support of the MTC and also 2 MCG. Despite a significant shortage of trained personnel and the absence of many mid-level staff, all assignments were able to proceed. When activating emergency aid to the Windward Islands following Hurricane Irma, 10 CSS SQN, partly due to the preparation for VJTF, was able to prepare and push out all necessary materials and supporting personnel within 24 hours via Eindhoven Airport and the port of Den Helder. 11 RSQN underwent parachute training in the first half of 2017 and supported 2 MCG with the Eagle Niala exercise. In the context of preparation for the VJTF(L), 11 RSQN participated in the ALERT EX in the Netherlands and the DEPLOY EX in Romania. After the summer leave, 11 RSQN was deployed as MSTU for emergency aid to the Windward Islands following the passage of Hurricane Irma. Shortly after the emergency aid, novices from the unit were able to participate in the mountain training. At the end of 2017, 11 RSQN prepared to provide 5 VPD teams starting January 1, 2018. Throughout the year, 11 RSQN was on standby in the context of the VJTF and the MSTU. 12 RSQN carried out various smaller activities in the first half of 2017 such as VPD deployment, boarding training in the Nieuwe Haven, Hunter Force, participation in the Cutlass Express exercise in Djibouti/Mauritius, support for training and exercises, and various ceremonial tasks including the Normandy commemoration. Furthermore, 12 RSQN phased out in the first half of 2017 to start with a newly formed crew in August 2018 for the preparation year. Due to insufficient outflow from the EMV, 12 RSQN began the preparation year with only two Troops instead of three. From August to October, functional training for the various specialists within the squadron, such as infantry engineers (IE), marksmen, and section commanders, was the focus. The unit also conducted SOP training during this period. In October-November, 12 RSQN participated in mountain training. Subsequently, the unit conducted shooting training in Otterburn, United Kingdom.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.53)
sections.text: 13 RSQN completed its training cycle in the first half of 2017. The squadron consisted of a staff and two Troops (due to underfilling during formation in 2016). Training during this period included winter training in Norway, SOUT training in Germany, Basic Helicopter Training, and fast rope training in the Netherlands, culminating in Maritime Interdiction Operations (MIO) training and MARSOC certification exercise. With the completion of the training cycle, 13 RSQN was certified MARC-4 in July 2017. In the second half of 2017, 13 RSQN conducted the Black Horse exercise at the US Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center in Twentynine Palms (Mojave Desert, California). The objective of this exercise was to conduct tactical shooting exercises up to squadron level. In the autumn, 13 RSQN carried out, among other things, the military tracker course in Aruba. For the CBMI mission, 13 RSQN assembled and trained a training team to be deployed in Iraq in January 2018. 14 CS SQN consists of three Troops: Anti Armour (AA) Troop, Armoured All Terrain Vehicle (AATV) Troop, and Assault Engineers (AE) Troop. Throughout 2017, these Troops followed their own training programs. AE and AATV supported, with each a section, the training year of a RSQN. As a result, they participated in several exercises of the training system, such as the mobility week and the certification exercise. AE also conducted cold weather training for Marines in Norway.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.54)
sections.text:
the Zr.Ms. Zeeland provided support during the operation. The Directie Operaties (Operations Directorate) also conducted several diverse national operations. For example, they were deployed twice before the summer, including for the search for a missing person. In August, they were deployed in Curaçao. As part of the MSTU, AE Troop provided emergency assistance in Sint Maarten after Hurricane Irma. 2017 concluded with a large MAST deployment in Hoogeveen. A characteristic of all these deployments was the short lead time between the request and the start of the operation. Another significant deployment involved FPME-4 in Jordan. The majority of the detachment consisted of marines from the 14 CS SQN, supplemented by a section from 11 RSQN. This assignment came unexpectedly and also had a short preparation time. 15 RSTA SQN completed the operational readiness according to the RSTA chain year in the first half of 2017. This included 1 Fire Support Team, 1 Mortar Section, 2 Recce Sniper Sections, 1 Raven Section, and the Joint Fires Cell being declared operationally ready. Among other exercises, the Team Centric Training, the Strike Module, the Military Operations in Urban Terrain (MOUT) training, and concluding with the Joint Fires Exercise Mamba were conducted. After the summer leave, a large portion of these units departed for the American Twentynine Palms for the Black Horse 2017 exercise. In this exercise, the units supported and underwent the tactical shooting exercise in addition to their own training. Furthermore, the Recce Sniper Troop formed the nucleus of the Enhanced Boarding Team for the Atalanta 2017 mission aboard Zr.Ms. Rotterdam. Outside of this deployment and Black Horse, units from 15 RSTA SQN remained active in the fall of 2017 and participated in various (purple) exercises. 

2nd Marine Combat Group (2 MCG) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) H.J. de Vries In 2017, 32 VPD were deployed, three rotations to Sint Maarten were completed, and Capacity Building Missions Iraq (CBMI) 7, 8, and 9 were conducted. The MCG staff achieved Operational Readiness status in the first half of 2017. In mid-2017, a Jungle Warfare Instructors Course was conducted in Belize, which also involved a platoon from the Air Mobile Brigade. Furthermore, various training activities of the sub-units were planned and executed. Due to the deployment of many personnel, the MCG primarily conducted small-scale exercises. Hurricane Irma led to a rapid deployment to Sint Maarten of the 2 MCG staff supported by personnel from 1 MCG, 11 RSQN, a Troop from 23 RSQN supplemented by units from the Air Mobile Brigade and engineers from the Royal Netherlands Army. An EBE was also deployed aboard Zr.Ms. Rotterdam in operation Atalanta. Finally, a Guard Team was deployed with Zr.Ms. Zeeland. They provided support from the Zr.Ms. Zeeland during the operation.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.55)
sections.text: The Operations Directorate also supported their mission in the Caribbean during hurricane relief efforts in Sint Maarten and Dominica. Netherlands Maritime Special Operation Forces (NLMARSOF) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) J. van Nee Caribbean as an underwater training location During the spring, the frogmen, placed within the operational squadrons of NLMARSOF, conducted the diving course 2017 in Curaçao. Unique to this training was the participation of operators from both M-squadron (National CT operations) and C-squadron (International SOF operations). Throughout this training, the most diverse aspects of SOF operations in a maritime environment were practiced. Port Defender The Port of Rotterdam served as the stage for this large port protection exercise for three days in the second week of April. Here, the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM), the Special Intervention Service (DSI), the Port of Rotterdam Authority, the Rotterdam Police Unit, and the Rotterdam-Rijnmond Safety Region trained together to be able to respond to a large-scale disaster or a terrorist attack in the port area of Rotterdam in the future. M-squadron participated in this exercise as part of the DSI and as a specialist in Maritime Counter Terrorism. Live Fire Exercises (LFX) M-squadron, NLMARSOF conducted two rotations of one week of LFX at the Sig Sauer Academy in Epping, United States. Due to the acquisition of the MCX weapon platform from Sig Sauer, M-squadron was able to utilize these facilities. During these weeks, they fired with this new weapon platform, and in the evening, a visit was made to the weapon factory to see how an MCX is made from a piece of lightweight metal. The Aptitude On Monday, June 26, at Van Ghent Barracks in Rotterdam; forty-two motivated marines are ready to begin the Aptitude. The first week primarily focuses on all physical requirements. Additionally, the basic knowledge and skills of the marines are also tested. Everyone had been informed in advance about the components and requirements for the Aptitude.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.56)
sections.text: The Operations Directorate received guidelines to use during the preparation. This naturally creates high expectations, but unfortunately, not everyone was equally well-prepared, and it was inevitable that some marines would drop out. The requirements based on the Defense Condition Test and the Physical Profile of Marines are 'hard' requirements. This means that there can be no compensations made and no exceptions granted. By the end of the first week, only twenty-two candidates remained in the running for a spot in the NLMARSOF training. Of these, five participants were exempt from the remaining Aptitude due to previously completed training, such as Mountain Leader and those who dropped out last year during the National Intervention Training. Seventeen marines stood in great uncertainty on the exercise ground in Doorn on the morning of Monday, July 3, waiting for what was to come. The following two weeks, an Operator from NLMARSOF jumps from a Hercules C-130 during an exercise.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.57)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-57 132 The Operations Directorate was approached differently than in previous years. This project was derived from the Danish SOF training. The emphasis during this two-week selection was primarily on individual qualities, with extensive testing of both physical and mental aspects. Two psychologists accompanied the entire selection process. Eleven candidates successfully completed these two weeks and were deemed suitable for the NLMARSOF training. Seabased Support Group (SSG) Commander: Major (majmarns) S. Peters In the past year, the Seabased Support Group (SSG) provided second-line logistical support in support of a challenging Operational Year Plan (OJP), combined with various 'real-world deployments'. This had a significant impact on the necessary personnel and material support. As a result, various specialists from SSG participated in exercises and 'real-world deployments' with other units to support them worldwide. This included logistics and munitions management, armaments technicians, communications service, and automotive mechanics. Due to the challenging OJP, the essential completion of an exercise or the execution of necessary maintenance on used materials was regularly under pressure. For some already scarce operational pool resources, this meant that they were less available for certain units. Surface Assault and Training Group (SATG) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) J.W. Scheltema, from July 11 Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) R.L. Posthumus First Landing Craft Task Unit (LCTU-1) This year was marked by the demobilization of the unit following its return from the EU operation Sophia. The maintenance of operational readiness was for the first time accompanied by the unit's completion of the FPM. Before the summer leave, the activities focused on supporting units and training. After the

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.58)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-58 133 Operations Directorate During the summer leave, particular attention was paid to the preparation for and execution of unit training. Training and Exercises In the first quarter, support was primarily provided to training units. For the initial military training of the marines, this meant the execution of the First Impressions for EMV 17-1 and the Finex of EMV 16-3. After conducting their own unit training, support was provided to the corporal training during the execution of their amphibious tasks. The second quarter brought a diverse range of activities. From early April, all units were engaged in completing the FPM. The non-commissioned officer training was supported, and thereafter the focus shifted to the 13th RSQN during the chain training. The emphasis during this training was on conducting MIO operations. Meanwhile, a composite unit provided support at the Jungle Warfare Course in Belize. The newly introduced Fast Support Craft were excellently tested in the challenging environment of the rainforest. Support for the remaining crew on the POTOM and the EMV brought the unit to summer leave. Jungle training in Belize.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.59)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-59 134 Operations Directorate The annual recurring support for the World Port Days was scheduled after this leave. Support for the chain training and the EMV was also provided in the third quarter. Finally, LCTU-1 conducted an educational training in Norway. Together with Norwegian units, both navigation and shooting exercises were carried out. This proved useful for the support in Rotterdam in the context of Host Nation Support. The security on the water during the transport of military material proceeded without significant incidents. Second Landing Craft Task Unit (LCTU-2) The first half of 2017 was focused on the preparation for LCTU-2. This unit was the second unit to be certified according to the intended preparation system. After the summer leave, the various assets of LCTU-2 undertook several serious deployments with Zr.Ms. Rotterdam during Operation Atalanta and emergency aid in the Caribbean with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman. Marines landing on the beaches of Texel.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.60)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-60 135 Operations Directorate Training and Exercises At the beginning of the year, the unit was not yet certified. Therefore, all training was focused on preparing and being ready for the certification moment in July. For the LCTU, the first joint training was a unit training at the Stuifdijk on Texel, where the Amphibious Beach Unit (ABU) was deployed and the vessels operated according to a Surface Assault (SURFALT) to and from the beach. At the end of February, the unit departed for ISHK to maintain individual skills and drills on various weapon systems. In March, the CERTIFEX for the 22nd RSQN took place. LCTU-2 had to support this training, which was also a good dress rehearsal for its own certification in July. The first part of the exercise took place in the vicinity of Vlissingen, using the Marine barracks as a Forward Operating Base (FOB). The second part of the exercise was at the Kop van Noord-Holland, where we operated from Zr.Ms. Rotterdam. After the CERTIFEX, LCTU-2 conducted some of its own training sessions. These included a training on Vlieland; a medical training and a communications week. Additionally, LCTU-2 repeated several annual activities in May and June, including the Military Basic Skills (MBV) and the FPM. LCTU-2 provided the amphibious demonstrations at the end of June during the Marine Days and SAIL Den Helder. Furthermore, the unit was responsible for coordination on the water. Subsequently, we proceeded to the CERTIFEX. During this CERTIFEX, not only the 11th RSQN was certified, but also LCTU-2. The setup was the same as in April. The training went well, and at the end of the training, we were officially certified and ready for deployment. The remainder of the unit provided support for the LC basic training and the MIO training of the 23rd RSQN. After the Landing Craft Task Element (LCTE) went on mission with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman, there was not much left of the LCTU, and the ABU recce conducted a reconnaissance in Norway. Various ABU units and small exercises were supported by us with personnel. The LCTE on board Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman completed a joint amphibious training with the 32nd RSQN in Aruba after the military assistance.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.61)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-61 136 Operations Directorate Operational Deployment At the beginning of the year, it became known that not the entire LCTU would accompany Zr.Ms. Rotterdam for the Atalanta mission off the Horn of Africa. The only components of LCTU-2 were the FRISC section and two communicators. From the moment this was announced, the FRISC section worked as closely as possible with Zr.Ms. Rotterdam to actually depart towards Somalia after the summer leave. During this mission, they conducted various patrols in cooperation with Swedish colleagues. On September 6, Hurricane Irma passed over the Leeward Islands, severely impacting Sint Maarten, Sint Eustatius, and Saba. Despite the presence of units on the islands, the devastation was so great that there was a need for additional personnel and equipment. For LCTU-2, this meant that the commander of the unit was flown in to assist and participate in the staff of the rotating elements, the 32nd and the 11th RSQN on the island. This support at the staff level lasted three weeks. Two weeks after Hurricane Irma, the decision was made to also send Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman to the Caribbean to provide humanitarian assistance. This decision was influenced by the fact that the now-passed Hurricane Maria had caused significant damage in Dominica. In addition to transporting many goods with Karel Doorman, an LCTE from LCTU-2 was also attached to the ship. This element included two Landing Craft Vehicle and Personnel (LCVPs) and a small staff. The LCTE carried out support by conducting various patrols in cooperation with the Coast Guard on Sint Maarten. A marine receives a compliment during the distribution of water on Sint Maarten.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.62)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-62 137 Operations Directorate The deployment was not limited to Sint Maarten; the LCTE was also deployed to Dominica to provide (humanitarian) assistance there. With the LCVPs, water was delivered to villages that were completely cut off from any form of aid and supply. Ultimately, the LCTE was on mission for almost three months and made various logistical trips in the area together with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman. FRISC Squadron Training and Exercises One of the primary tasks of the FRISC Squadron is to provide vessels for FRISC training and to supply personnel and vessels for the various task assignments of the LCTUs. In addition, the FRISC Squadron trained intensively throughout the year with MARSOF units for the national task regarding maritime counter-terrorism. Furthermore, attention was also paid to intensifying cooperation with MARSOF in the area of training for conventional support during operations on and over water. Group Leaders Klein Bovenwater (KBW) and Mine Service Group Leader: Captain (ktz) ir. J. Franken, from December 13 Captain (ktz) H.J.F. Toebast In 2017, the CZSK had the following 'large' KBW units: six mine countermeasure vessels: Zr.Ms. Makkum, Zr.Ms. Schiedam, Zr.Ms. Urk, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen, Zr.Ms. Willemstad, and Zr.Ms. Zierikzee, as well as two hydrographic survey vessels: Zr.Ms. Luymes and Zr.Ms. Snellius and the torpedo works ship: Zr.Ms. Mercuur. The 'small' KBW fleet consists of diving vessels, tugboats, LCVPs, Landing Craft Utility (LCU), FRISCs, the Marine Training Vessel (MOV) Van Kinsbergen, and Zr.Ms. Urania. Assembly and Upgrading The minehunters Zr.Ms. Makkum, Zr.Ms. Willemstad, and Zr.Ms. Urk underwent the upgrading process in 2017, and Zr.Ms. Makkum and Zr.Ms. Willemstad completed the operational readiness test at the MCMVOST in Zeebrugge.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.63)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-63 138 Directorate of Operations Operational activities Zr.Ms. Schiedam and Zr.Ms. Makkum were part of NATO's permanent mine countermeasures squadron in 2017: SNMCMG1. Zr.Ms. Mercuur, Zr.Ms. Schiedam, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen, and Zr.Ms. Willemstad participated in the exercise Eager Archer 2017, the Midshipmen's Cruise led by NLMAFOR MCM. This annual trip was combined with the exercise Baltops 17. During this trip, the ships visited ports including Stavanger. Equipment In 2017, Zr.Ms. Urk and Zr.Ms. Zierikzee underwent Named Maintenance in Zeebrugge under the coordination of the Binational Support Team (BST). Personnel In 2017, the Group Senior Mine Service and Small Above Water (GOMD) conducted several work visits to Zr.Ms. Schiedam during her deployment in SNMCMG1, and to Zr.Ms. Makkum, Zr.Ms. Mercuur, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen, and Zr.Ms. Willemstad during the Midshipmen's Cruise. The staff of the GOMD expanded with an additional officer for WSM and now consists of four people (Chief of the Crew, two Weapon System Management officers, and Ship Manager in Conservation) and the Binational Support Team with 11 Dutch personnel remotely in Zeebrugge. The staff developed future mine countermeasures policy in anticipation of the replacement of the current Alkmaar-class mine countermeasures vessels. An important part of this policy is mine countermeasures at greater distances from the mother ship using underwater, surface, and aerial drones. The staff also initiated a plan to bring the DDG back under the Mine Service to improve efficiency and clear responsibility within the mine countermeasures organization. On March 21, the Chief of the Crew of Hr.Ms. Urk, SMJRODOPS Berentsen, was awarded the 'De Ruyter Medal' by Minister of Infrastructure and Water Management M. Schultz van Haegen, in recognition of the significant commitment and involvement of the Mine Service in maritime operations. On April 21, the team from the broad mine countermeasures community became champions in rowing. The GOMD staff organized a very successful Mine Service reunion on May 17 for actively serving personnel, veterans, and former members, which also included the former mine sweepers Naaldwijk and Mahu from the Floating Heritage Royal Netherlands Navy.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.64)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-64 139 Operations Directorate Submarine Service Group Leader: Captain (ktz) H.M.T. de Groot This year was again characterized by an intensive sailing program for the Submarine Service. The voyages took its boats and crews this year from the Mediterranean Sea to Norwegian waters and back to the Atlantic Ocean. As in every previous year, the first major commitment of 2017 was the facilitation of the NLSMCC by Zr.Ms. Walrus. After the summer, the crew of Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw worked hard on the training trajectory. Operational deployment was again an important part of the Submarine Service's tasks this year. Additionally, participation in necessary international exercises took place throughout the year. Naval Aviation Service (MLD) Group Leader: Commander (cdr) G.A. Polet The increasing availability of NH90 helicopters continued in 2017. With this upward trend, expertise in the Netherlands also increased, positioning our country at the forefront among NH90 users worldwide. However, the large number of different configurations still negatively impacted availability, as various components were insufficiently stocked. Meanwhile, the update of the NH90 from Full Operational Capable (FOC) to Full Radar Capable (FRC) and Maintenance Release 1 (MR1) continued. This latest upgrade is still taking place in Italy during the Retrofit. With the increasing availability, we were also able to meet more of the demand for NH90 on board ships during deployments. Operations This year, a total of 1968 flight hours were performed with the NH90 helicopter. Additionally, our simulator was still in Italy, where we trained a total of 998 hours that year. The first half of the year was partly focused on supporting Zr.Ms. Evertsen in its training trajectory (SARC-4 & NOST), followed by an SNMG1 deployment from May 8 to July 13 with the N319. Part of this deployment included participation in exercises such as BALTOPS and Dynamic Mongoose. From March 4 to June 17, the N324 was deployed on board Zr.Ms. van Amstel during SSCG1. The ship was relieved in the Caribbean by Zr.Ms. Zeeland for SSCG2. In the OPV concept, where the patrol vessel was supported by 2 FRISC’s and an NH90 helicopter, the added value of an NH90 as a game-changer was once again proven. On board was the N325, which was embarked for the period from June 19 to November 10.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.66)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-66 141 Operations Directorate Maritime Warfare Centre (MWC) Commander: Captain (ktz) C.M. Vooijs The year 2017 was marked by a turnaround in the financial situation of Defense. Various motions, including that of Member of Parliament C.G. van der Staaij (SGP), freed up budget for selective strengthening. To provide direction for this, the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) issued the Sailplan 2030, which set a goal for operational readiness of the organization and the strengthening of niche capabilities. The necessity to enhance the knowledge base was evident and was therefore addressed. In this overview, we highlight only a few highlights from 2017. The MWC projected the existing template of the defense doctrine discussions onto CZSK. Based on VCZSK 007 Doctrine Development, the doctrine committee of the Royal Netherlands Navy (DCKM) was established under the chairmanship of the Chief of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (PC-CZSK) as a counterpart to the Doctrine Committee of the Armed Forces (DCK). This committee is intended to guide the development of operational knowledge products of CZSK. This involves standardization (doctrine, the way we currently perform our tasks) and concept development (future task execution). Logically, MWC retains the coordinating role in these activities, but the Commander of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (C-ZSK) took ownership of the steering of that process. Associated with this was a new department for Change Management and Innovation, which was strongly connected in communication with MWC.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.67)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-67 142 Operations Directorate For the coordination of the external development of knowledge, MWC has been contributing to the Knowledge Network Sea for several years, together with S&A. This body, under the leadership of DMO, aligns the national development of specific scientific knowledge and technology for the benefit of CZSK, particularly within the Golden Triangle (Defense, Industry, Knowledge Institutions). The increasing political demand for international cooperation means that projects in NATO funds such as PESCO, but especially the EU Defence Fund, must also be coordinated. In addition, the national coordination of activities from the growing number of maritime Centres of Excellence means that the Knowledge Network Sea is becoming an increasingly important forum to maintain oversight and provide direction for external knowledge development. Operational highlights this year to which MWC made a significant contribution include: Exercise Formidable Shield 2017, the participation of Zr.Ms. De Ruyter in live multinational BMD scenarios under the command of USN 6th Fleet. JPOW 2017; participation with a SIM-LCF in a multinational BMD exercise organized in collaboration between Germany and the Netherlands. Field briefing during jungle training in Belize.

sections.text: Operations Directorate The First of Class Firing of the Mk 48 Mod 7 AT by Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw. Among the niches to be developed is the Maritime Ballistic Missile Defense (MBMD) capability, which has been under consideration for some time. A DMP-A identified the need for a sensor on board the LCFs, but to generate a truly operational Early Warning Capability for ballistic missiles, a complete set of prerequisites must be fulfilled. To this end, the AR decided to establish an introduction committee, for which MWC would provide the framework. This IC-MBMD must coordinate the generation of prerequisites and simultaneously demonstrate and integrate the capability in the Integrated Air and Missile Defence systems of NATO during periodic exercises such as Formidable Shield (FS) and JPOW. H-MWC is the chair, and a new MBMD section under the Department of Doctrine and Tactics is carrying out the working group actions. The JKCMOX is working hard on the development of military-wide regulations regarding Working at Height within Defense. The knowledge center plays a pioneering role for the other OPCOs in this regard. The result is that they have decided to use the methodology employed by JKCMOX as the standard. By providing instructors for various training courses, JKCMOX ensures knowledge retention within the MOX domains at Defense. Examples include support for the Sign Awareness Instructor Course in Reek and the Jungle Warfare Instructor Course conducted in Belize. By incorporating input from various After Action Reports into new instructions, JKCMOX enhances the safety of training, exercises, and operations in the MOX domain. The aforementioned motion by Van der Staaij and the MBMD initiative led to some strengthening of the MWC organization. An information manager and a cyber officer were added to the organization, and (partially through reorganization) a BMD section was formed. The strengthened organization continued to produce knowledge products, the most notable of which were: Functional Concept Air and Missile Defense Green Paper Low Frequency Active and Passive Sonar Advisory Note on the establishment of C-IED organization Handbook on Boarding Operations Handbook on Military Operations in the Mountains BEL/NLD Handbook on MCM operations.

Civil Production After the completion of the SHIP2 project at the end of 2016, the new system was further evaluated and put into use in 2017. This department generated the first depth images from the new database for depth storage and processed these into the products. A total of 69 new ENC cells were published, along with twelve paper nautical charts and four 1800 atlases for the corresponding area. Thus, all 1800 atlases have now been produced from the new Hydrographic Production Database (HPD). Additionally, the annual editions of HP7, HP1D, HP33, and HP33D were published.
