These charts were published in December.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.72)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-72 147 Operations Directorate It is of great importance to have up-to-date information. Especially in the Caribbean, this remains a point of ongoing attention. Two cartographers therefore made a working visit to the Leeward Islands. Due to Hurricane Irma, the Windward Islands were not visited. The visit was successful. Not only were agreements made to better secure the information provision in the future, but a wealth of information was also gathered. Participation was made in the Hydrographic Services and Standards Committee (HSSC) and various related working groups under the IHO framework. In addition, we held working meetings with colleagues from neighboring countries. At the request of the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management (I&M), a staff member from the service participated in a working group under the Sub-Committee on Navigation, Communications and Search and Rescue (NCSR) of the IMO. This working group assesses proposals for routing measures (new traffic separation schemes, etc.) submitted by IMO member states. The service participates in this as a subject matter expert. Geodesy and Tides The Knowledge Center for Geodesy & Tides (KCG&G) section provides knowledge for the measurement processes and publications of the Hydrographic Service, as well as for other branches of defense and government. The geodetic expertise is applied at sea, where the water level is of great importance. Tide knowledge is linked to marine geodesy. An important application is determining the correct coordinate systems and enabling conversions between them. This concerns both horizontal and vertical references. Another application is providing geodetic and tide data for general use, such as calculating boundaries at sea and publishing tide predictions. Support for Hydrographic Publications KCG&G hosted the Data Quality Working Group (DQWG) from May 13 to 15 at the Frederikkazerne in The Hague. The DQWG is a working group of the HSSC of the IHO. The working group is responsible for developing a standard for representing the quality of hydrographic products. Finland transferred the chairmanship of this working group to the Netherlands for a period of three years.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.73)
sections.text: 148 Directorate of Operations At the initiative of the Netherlands, the HSSC approved new Terms of Reference for the DQWG during the annual meeting from November 9 to 10 in Ottawa, Canada. Its objective is now to ensure that aspects of data quality are applied in an appropriate and harmonized manner within future IHO standards. Additionally, the KCG&G participated in the Tides, Water Levels and Currents Working Group (TWCWG) from May 8 to 12 in Victoria, Canada. The TWCWG is another working group of the HSSC. The goal of this working group is to develop a standard for the delivery and representation of surface currents and vertical reference levels. The standard to be developed is based on components of the S-100 product specifications. Support for hydrographic surveys An internal project has been initiated to clarify the relationship between the planned, executed, delivered, and published hydrographic surveys. This research will lead to a better understanding of the effort required to measure the current seabed position and the observation of significant objects on the seabed, as well as the eventual publication in the navigation chart. The result is expected by the end of 2018. Work on the bridge of Zr.Ms. Snellius.

Mollema (HOV-A) from January 1 Lt. Commander (ltz1) S.M. Duineveld (HOV-B) from January 1 to May 2 Lt. Commander (ltz1) S.R. Maureau (HOV-B) from May 2 The first weeks after the holidays, Zr.Ms. Snellius was undergoing maintenance. From January 30, it resumed collecting hydrographic data. At that time, the ship operated on a rotation schedule of two crews, the A-crew and the B-crew. Although conducting hydrographic days is core business for a hydrographic survey vessel, general proficiency for the ship's crew is also necessary to ensure safe working and living conditions on board. To train this proficiency, a CT is scheduled once a year, conducted under the inspiring leadership of one of the MOST teams. The B-crew had the honor of kicking off at the end of February, followed by the A-crew a few weeks later. The A-crew combined this training with a port visit to Antwerp, after which the sailing program continued. After these educational periods, it was time to conduct some hydrographic days, interspersed with a number of foreign ports for necessary relaxation. Thus, the B-crew visited Newcastle in June. This port was also at the top of the A-crew's list of foreign ports to visit. Consequently, the ship visited Newcastle again in July in a short time, now with the A-crew on board. Stavanger was the port visited in the autumn by the A-crew, where a visit to the Preikestolen was, of course, a must. Afterwards, the B-crew then visited Stavanger. By early November, the sailing days were over, and Zr.Ms. Snellius went to Delfzijl for maintenance for the rest of the year.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.77)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-77 152 Operations Directorate Zr.Ms. Luymes (A803) Commanders: Lieutenant Commander (ltz1) J.P. Lokerse (Crew C) from January 1, Lieutenant Commander (ltz1) S.R. Maureau (Crew B) from November 13. From the beginning of the year until January 17, Zr.Ms. Luymes was in Harlingen for the execution of multi-year maintenance. Damen Shiprepair carried this out. After the maintenance in Harlingen, Zr.Ms. Luymes returned to Den Helder on January 17 to undergo the final part of the maintenance at the Marinebedrijf. On March 8, 2017, Zr.Ms. Luymes moved from berth 62 to berth 11. Following the maintenance, a training period commenced to restore operational, personnel, and material readiness by completing the training trajectory Safety and Readiness Checks (SARC-1 to 3). SARC-4 took place from April 24 to 26. The Belgian-Dutch MOST provided the leadership and training for this and also assessed the crew's capabilities. During this period, various exercises were conducted, such as maneuvering, navigation, and fire drills. On May 2, Zr.Ms. Luymes departed for sea; however, it had to return to Den Helder on May 3 due to problems with the diesel generators. These issues were resolved on May 7, and the ship returned to operational area HY17201. This was located in the shipping lane north of the Wadden Islands. Zr.Ms. Luymes was part of the group of ships that opened to the public during SAIL Den Helder from June 22 to 25. On Sunday, June 25, the ship departed for sea in connection with the exercise Sandy Coast, in which it would participate until July 5. For the exercise, Zr.Ms. Luymes placed various exercise mines at predetermined positions on the seabed. Several minehunters found these during the exercise and were subsequently picked up by Zr.Ms. Luymes with the help of divers. The diving team also brought a decompression tank on board. In the remaining time between placing and picking up the exercise mines, surveying was conducted in the operational area HY17201. Five days later, Zr.Ms. Luymes departed for ten days at sea for hydrographic work. Just like earlier in 2017, there were standby watches during this trip.

sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-78 153 Operations Directorate officers and hydrographers temporarily filled the personnel shortage. Upon returning to Den Helder, the log and the magnetic compass were calibrated. The crew conducted sounding operations from August 15 to August 23 in HY17201. During this period, the ship went to Den Helder to take on the new Chief of the Crew and there was a change of the watch officers. On September 4, Zr.Ms. Luymes departed towards Brünsbuttel for the Northern Coasts (NOCO) exercise, where the vessel served as the flagship. Sailing in a formation with Zr.Ms. Schiedam, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen, and BNS Narcis, they reached Karlskrona, Sweden on September 8. From Friday, September 8 to Monday, September 11, the crew had time for final preparations for the exercise and some Rest and Recreation in Karlskrona. After this port visit, the NOCO exercise commenced. The ship deployed various exercise mines, which were subsequently searched for by the minehunters. At the end of the exercise, from September 22 to September 25, a port visit was made to the capital of Denmark, Copenhagen, for Rest and Recreation. On September 29, Zr.Ms. Luymes docked again in Den Helder. Following the NOCO exercise, there were three periods during which the ship operated midweek. During two of these periods, hydrography students from the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz (MIWB) in Terschelling were embarked to familiarize them with the hydrographic tasks of Zr.Ms. Luymes and life at sea. Their supervisor was the former Chief of the Hydrographic Service F.P.J. de Haan. To verify our current method of tide reduction and to allow the students to experience how to deploy a tide gauge buoy, this was done in the new work area HY17516. This area has 45 effective sounding days and is located just above the northernmost traffic separation scheme, bordering British waters. From October 23 to October 27 and from October 30 to November 9, the C-crew was active in this area. On November 13, the B-crew transferred their belongings from Zr.Ms. Snellius to Zr.Ms. Luymes to subsequently operate in a two-on-two off schedule with the C-crew. On November 15, the B-crew departed to sea with Zr.Ms. Luymes. They conducted sounding operations in a combined area HY17108_229_209, after which they began work in area HY17225. This area is located south of the approach to Rotterdam at Steenbank Vessel Traffic Service. On November 18, she

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.79)
sections.text: The Operations Directorate directed Zr.Ms. Luymes to Vlissingen via the Oostgat, to anchor in the roadstead of Vlissingen and shelter from the stormy weather. During the time the ship was anchored, the crew continued to collect data with the hydrographic boat. On November 21, Zr.Ms. Luymes moored again in Den Helder. During the transit to Den Helder, the Multibeam Echosounder was tested near IJmuiden. Due to the bad weather, the departure of the C crew was postponed, and they left for sea on December 1. Because of the still marginal conditions in the North, the ship began operations in area HY18115 just above the Wadden Islands. On December 4, Zr.Ms. Luymes returned. The B crew set sail on December 11 and returned on December 20. The final loading operations in work area HY17108_209_229 were carried out, and the work continued in HY17225. Due to the bad weather, they diverted to Zeebrugge in Belgium during this period. From December 13 to 16, they were alongside waiting for better weather. As soon as conditions improved, Zr.Ms. Luymes first went to HY17110_116 and then again to HY17225. Finally, the hydrographic year was concluded with a patch test with the boat.

sections.title: Directie Materiële Instandh (p.12)
sections.text: Directorate of Material Maintenance The reorganization of various defense components also played a role at the barracks. On June 1, the largest user at the barracks, the Services Center Recruitment & Selection, transitioned to a new organization. It continues under the name Services Center Personnel Logistics (DC-PL). This transition had two crucial consequences. The organization grew significantly, and the accommodation in buildings 028-029 became very cramped. Additionally, the defense inspection protocol was revamped, giving the MEA sports instructors a direct role in it. This resulted in a considerable extra burden for the barracks and all available sports facilities. Thanks in part to all the challenges that arose, the staff, together with local supporters such as DBBO, PARESTO, and FBD, were able to demonstrate this year what the MEA can do and what significance it holds for CZSK, Defense, and the city of Amsterdam. Events in 2017 Right from the first week of January, the MEA operated at full capacity. The first conference was immediately one of the larger gatherings that took place this year in the event center. This was the NATO Maritime Operations Working Group. This conference had a special aspect; exceptionally, all partners of the conference participants were also accommodated at the barracks. A limited ladies' program also took place. Unfortunately, the participants of this MAROPSWG could not be motivated to join the annual New Year's run of the barracks, a sporting event where participation is more important than winning and where prizes are determined by lottery. This year, it was also noted that the number of visitors was nearly the same as in previous years. A total of 33,135 visitors were welcomed during 983 events and reservations. In addition to MAROPSWG, various large NATO conferences, symposia, and sports events were hosted, including the Military World Championship in Basketball. The barracks also served multiple times as the host location for the Admiralty Council, which conducted the three-day retreat at the MEA, during which the Sail Plan 2030 and the future of the Royal Netherlands Navy in general were discussed. This year, shared use of the conference facilities by civilian partners was again arranged by the Project Bureau Marine Terrain Amsterdam, but unfortunately, this was minimally utilized. Accommodation This year, over fifteen thousand reservations for Short-Term Accommodation were processed for activities at and around the MEA.

sections.text: 6_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-15 170 Directorate of Material Maintenance On August 25, the command transfer of CKM took place. Brigadier General (bg) F. van Sprang handed over command to his counterpart Mac Mootry. During his speech, Mac Mootry stated that “Staying relevant, delivering quality, and thereby successfully completing assignments remains the course. When we are called upon, we move forward and get the job done. Can do and will do!” In September, the Corps Commander opened two new barracks buildings at the base. The names of the buildings refer to missions of the Corps of Marines: Cop Tabar refers to operations in Afghanistan, and Op Zuc (observation post) refers to the Mount Igman mission in former Yugoslavia. The Marines' tradition room was also opened, where the flag of the Corps of Marines received a permanent place on the first floor near the cabin in the main building. The year was, as usual, concluded with the celebration of the Corps anniversary and the laying of a wreath at the Oostplein. The wreath-laying commemorates fallen marines. The Corps anniversary was organized for the first time for all actively serving marines across the Corps in Rotterdam. CKM opened the Corps anniversary with video contact with the marines deployed in Iraq. Additionally, in the last weeks, there were the traditional study days with which we concluded 2017. Naval Base Vlissingen (MKVLIS) Commander: Lt. Commander (ltz1) H.W.M. Veldhuizen In 2017, there was no need for the main task, which is accommodating CZSK ship crews, just as in previous years. After Zr.Ms. Evertsen in 2015, no CZSK units have been in Vlissingen for maintenance or new construction, resulting in stagnation of the accommodation of ship crews. The fact that this task has not been fulfilled does not mean that the Naval Base Vlissingen (MKVLIS) has not experienced activities. In 2017, we again saw a shift in tasks towards a more general, facilitating character. As a result, the current two core tasks for the base in Vlissingen consist primarily of facilitating and supporting a large number of exercises for CZSK units and other military components. The second core task involves collaborating and networking with government agencies and the business community for the purpose of the new barracks to be built in 2021. The closing date of MKVLIS is April 1, 2018.

sections.text: 6_KM_Annual_Report_2017_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-18 173 Directorate of Material Maintenance (VBHKAZ). This was especially true as the Marines were prepared for the VJTF this year. The designated unit must be ready for deployment within 48 hours after the Notice to Move is issued. Therefore, equipment and supplies were prepared for the VJTF. The units trained on and from the barracks. Additionally, there was also a serious deployment. After Hurricane Irma struck Sint Maarten in September, personnel and equipment were also deployed from Doorn to provide initial relief in the West. The VBHKAZ facilitated four command transfers in 2017. The Sea-based Support Group (SSG), the First Marine Combat Group (1MCG), the MTC, and the barracks staff received a new commander. Just like the commanders of 2MCG and NLMARSOF, the newcomers were given a crash course on 'handling hazardous materials'. Every workshop and storage location was thoroughly checked for possible deficiencies. Teams with personnel from all units conducted clean sweeps. Meanwhile, the numerous transport movements continued for the intensive training program of the OPE MARNS. The vehicles and containers of the units were accompanied on the exercise terrain by containers from the moving company and vans from contractors. The barrack buildings Fak Fak (non-commissioned officers) and Algiers (troops) received a facelift. The flooring was renewed, the walls were painted, the ceilings were replaced, and new lighting was installed. Several hundred colleagues temporarily moved to another barrack room for this purpose. Furniture and other goods were temporarily stored. A carousel of logistical movements within the barracks had to seamlessly align with the training and deployment program. The meeting rooms Norway, Assen, and De Punt were also refurbished and equipped with new furniture and MULAN computers with projectors. This also applied to the Congress Hall, which received an entirely new sound system. Pantries were built in building Sisophon. The Old Sick Bay and the Old Sick Room were converted into storage rooms and equipped with shower facilities. A shelter was constructed in the garden of the Gouden Bal. In building Chatham, twelve additional flexible workspaces were created. The classrooms were re-carpeted and furnished. During the winter leave, a temporary accommodation was set up in the parking lot between the Cafeteria and the Congress Hall, complete with locker rooms and fully furnished barrack rooms. Meanwhile, work continued diligently on the 'output specification' for the MARKAZ to be built in Vlissingen. Although the process is still on schedule for a move.

sections.title: Directie Materiële Instandh (p.22)
sections.text: On March 15, the Directorate of Materiel Maintenance Noorderkwartier signed the Letter of Intent for the Exploration of Sustainable Heat Supply in Den Helder to explore the possibilities for a sustainable heating network. For the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM), the head of the Maritime Support Department, Captain (ktz) R.J.A.M. Ramaekers, signed. This collaboration gives a good push to the municipality of Den Helder's goal of becoming an energy-neutral municipality by 2040. A sustainable heating network contributes to a significant reduction in CO₂ emissions. The research aims to obtain an overview of all possibilities as well as to assess feasibility. Part of the study involves the use of sustainable sources such as geothermal heat. If the research yields positive results, the existing heating network at the Nieuwe Haven, which is maintained and managed by the EDB, can be connected in the future. In April, the Energy Management System project was initiated. This project was initiated by the European Defence Agency (EDA) and aims to save energy within Defence. Such pilots are being conducted in nine countries. In the Netherlands, the Nieuwe Haven was chosen as a pilot because it accounts for 30 percent of the total energy consumption of Defence. The scope of the pilot includes the eight largest consuming buildings at Willemsoord and the energy plant combined heat and power station (KWS) of the EDB. Since the company has consumption figures at the building level and much expertise in energy consumption, Mr. R.J.L. Put from the EDB is the project leader. Mr. M. Gijsbers from the Executive Staff is the project leader for the entire project. If the pilot is successful, the project will be rolled out across Defence. On October 1, the Combined Heat and Power Station, the energy plant at the Nieuwe Haven, celebrated its 25th anniversary. This was celebrated on September 26 at the station's premises with the employees of the EDB and their partners. Electricity consumption has grown 2.5 times in 25 years, but the objectives of the Combined Heat and Power Station remain the same as at the beginning: emergency power plant for the Defence locations in Den Helder, transformer station to provide ships with 60 Hz electricity and buildings with 50 Hz, as well as electricity production at times when consumption exceeds what the grid operator can supply. When the plant was designed in the 1980s, it was decided to also produce electricity daily for peak loads and to use the heat in a district heating system at the Nieuwe Haven. As automation has increasingly played a role, on August 28, 2017, a position for Chief Technician was converted into System Administrator Process Automation.

During Prinsjesdag on the third Tuesday of September, the general public could enjoy festive march music through The Hague, the shining ceremonial uniforms, and the historical glamour of the armed forces. As usual, the Marine Band had the honorable task of playing the Wilhelmus upon the arrival of our monarch at the Binnenhof. At the invitation of the German Bundeswehr, the Marine Band and Drummers & Pipers were guests at the International Tattoo 'Musikfest der Bundeswehr' in Düsseldorf on September 23, after which six performances followed at the National Tattoo in Rotterdam Ahoy back in the Netherlands. The anniversary of the Marine Corps was musically celebrated with a large concert on November 7 at the Doelen in Rotterdam. Here, presenter Lieutenant Commander (kltz) W.A. Kramer guided the audience through the program featuring surprising and colorful soloists such as S. Trkulja and Latin singer R. Sanchez.

sections.text: 183 Directorate of Material Maintenance and the family tours, which were well received by the public. The museum also played an active role during the major events in Den Helder. sections.title: Directie Materiële Instandh (p.29)
sections.text: 6_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-29 184 Directorate of Material Maintenance 50 + fair in Utrecht. The museum received several special objects for the collection through donations, such as the ship's bell from submarine KXVIII, a watercolor by H.M. Krabbé from 1903, a plaque from the National Youth Association from the wreck of the cruiser De Ruyter, the officer's whistle of R. Crommelin - first officer on board the destroyer Hr.Ms. Kortenaer during the Battle of the Java Sea - and the gavel of the Marine Society 'Modderlust' in Surabaya. The museum received 95,202 visitors. Training Vessels Naval Training Vessel Van Kinsbergen The ship primarily sailed for the KIM to train the cadets for the Naval Service. Additionally, it operated for the DVS and the MIWB in Terschelling. The ship had the following sailing periods. The year began with the first Sea practicals for the cadets from January 23 to February 19. During these weeks, the ship was in Kiel on Sundays and in Aalborg during the week. The second period involved training the non-commissioned officers for ZWST-K, from March 13 to March 20. The vessel visited the port of Aarhus during the week. The third sailing period was the second practical period for the cadets. This was from April 3 to April 30. On Sundays, the ship was in Kiel, and during the week, the ship was in Copenhagen. From May 7 to June 1, the Van Kinsbergen was in Terschelling for two different periods and sailed with students from the MIWB. The last trip before the summer leave was again for the purpose of training cadets. During this trip, the ship made a large round trip through the Baltic Sea. The ship visited several ports there during that period. During the visit to Karlskrona, the cadets rowed against students from the Swedish equivalent of the KIM. In Finnish waters, a Finnish liaison officer was on board, and the cadets and crew visited the Finnish KIM. After the summer leave, the ship made two more trips. The first was from September 25 to October 7 as a resit period for the cadets and the ZWST-K training. During this period, the ship spent one day in Kiel, Flensburg, and Aarhus. The last period was from October 23 to November 25. During this time, the ship again sailed for the cadets during their third practical period. The vessel was in Kiel on Sundays and alternated between Odense, Fredericia, and Sonderborg during the week.

sections.title: Directie Materiële Instandh (p.30)
sections.text: 6_KM_Annual_Report_2017_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-30 185 Directorate of Material Maintenance Zr.Ms. Urania Commander: LtCdr (ltz1) W.W. Wester After its annual maintenance at the Van der Hoeven shipyard, which was completed on February 8, further preparations for the 2017 sailing season could take place in Den Helder. After Seatrain Command also gave approval, the sailing season began with a training week for cadets in the Wadden Sea and North Sea. Aspects such as current, wind, and tide were central during this training week. Subsequently, the ship sailed to Rotterdam for the Race of the Classics for students. Cadets from the Royal Naval Institute (KIM) formed the crew for this race, during which the ship won the "Sprint Cup." In May and June, the ship also conducted navigation training, for which it sailed to the southern coast of Britain and the Channel Islands. Since this year marked the 350th anniversary of Michiel de Ruyter's famous raid on the Medway with the Dutch fleet, Zr.Ms. Urania, following in the footsteps of our former fleet guardian, repeated this voyage on June 8. However, it had to endure a rare June storm in the English Channel before it could begin its journey towards Chatham from the French coast. During the crossing of the Channel, Urania experienced some time with an unclear propeller, causing it to drift away from its course to clear its rigging. After the commemoration in Chatham, the ship sailed via London to the Netherlands to attend SAIL Den Helder. This was also a precursor to numerous festivals in the Baltic Sea. In July and August, the Tall Ship Races were on the agenda. These took the ship through Sweden deep into the Gulf of Finland. The return journey went via Lithuania to the final finish in Poland. The crew during this race consisted of Dutch, Belgian, Swedish, and German cadets. After a period of VIP trips from Enkhuizen, the year was once again concluded with the Race of the Classics for Young Professionals, in which "Young Defense" provided the crew. At the beginning of November, the ship was delivered in Drimmelen for its fourth and possibly last maintenance period at the Van der Hoeven shipyard.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.3)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean General In 2017, CZMCARIB served as a training area for both maritime and land exercises and took action in the fight against illegal activities at sea. In the second half of the year, special military assistance was requested, which ultimately resulted in a CZMCARIB-wide support operation. On September 6, Hurricane Irma passed over the Leeward Islands of Sint Maarten, Saba, and Sint Eustatius. It left a trail of destruction, with the former island being the hardest hit. Training and Support A variety of exercises and training sessions took place in the Caribbean over the past year. These were aimed at maintaining the operational readiness of the own units, but also served as an ideal training location for CZSK, CLSK, and CLAS units or partners in the region. In addition to its own training, CZMCARIB also supported training for important strategic partners in the Caribbean; the United States and France. The CZMCARIB units also trained abroad: at the American Camp Lejeune (Military Operations in Urban Terrain) and in French Guiana and Martinique (unit cohesion training). The Fight Against Drugs Prompt action to ensure safety at sea and from the sea required continuous vigilance. CZMCARIB is a '24/7 organization' where the Operations Center of the Maritime Headquarters Caribbean is staffed 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. 2017 yielded several operational successes, resulting in approximately 7000 kg of contraband being removed from the trade market. Arrival of the station ship Zr.Ms. Van Amstel in Curaçao.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.4)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Area Work Visit In 2017, various dignitaries visited the Caribbean area for a work visit. They are listed here in chronological order. Commander 13 LtBrig, Major General G. Koot Commander of the Royal Marechaussee, Lieutenant General H. van den Brink Director of Operations CZSK and Commander of the Marine Corps, Brigadier General F.V. van Sprang Minister of Foreign Affairs, A.G. Koenders Minister of Security and Justice, S.A. Blok The Royal Army and the Royal Navy conduct joint exercises in Curaçao. International Drug Enforcement In addition to the external defense of six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in upholding the international rule of law in the Caribbean area. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The Navy is closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization 'Joint Interagency Task Force South' based in Key West. The Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Area is therefore the commander of Task Group 4.4., one of the task groups of this organization.

Corveleijn EMSD The Maritime Headquarters Caribbean (MHKC) coordinated and directed this year as the operational center in the Caribbean all operations and exercises of the military units present in the West and a growing number of visiting domestic and foreign units. The most significant coordination of deployment was the emergency relief operation for the islands affected by Hurricane Irma in the Leeward Islands and Dominica. Additionally, the MHKC frequently acted as the Commander of Military Resources (CMM) for various military assistance requests from the local governments of the islands in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. The execution of main task 3, support of civil authorities, has significantly increased in recent years at CZMCARIB, thereby supporting the vision of becoming the maritime and security partner in the Caribbean. Station Ships This year, four ships were placed under the command of C-ZMCARIB as SSCG. Throughout the year, Zr.Ms. Holland, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel, Zr.Ms. Zeeland, and Zr.Ms. Van Speijk carried out the various tasks of the SSCG within the command area of CZMCARIB. All units were equipped with an NH90 onboard helicopter, which acted as a force multiplier in the various operations.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.6)
sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Counter Drugs All station ships have patrolled for both the Caribbean Coast Guard (KWCARIB) and for CTG 4.4. Various successes were achieved in this regard. In cooperation with international units, CTG 4.4 removed approximately 7000 kg of contraband from the trade market in 2017. In the international operations, cooperation took place with various countries including the United States, France, Colombia, the United Kingdom, and the Dominican Republic. Hurricane Relief In preparation for the hurricane season, which runs from June 1 to November 30, the annual Hurricane Exercise was conducted by CZMCARIB in collaboration with local authorities in the Leeward Islands. The importance of this exercise was demonstrated by the subsequent passages of various hurricanes through the Caribbean Sea. On September 6, Hurricane Irma passed over the Leeward Islands, leaving a trail of destruction. In preparation for the actual passage, the 32 Raiding Squadron (32RSQN) was prepositioned from Aruba to Sint Maarten, Saba, and Sint Eustatius. Additionally, Zr.Ms. Zeeland (including NH90), Zr.Ms. Pelikaan, and part of the Company in the West (CIDW) were made ready to provide assistance. Patrol of Marines a day after the hurricane in Sint Maarten.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.7)
sections.text: Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied. The DASH-8 patrol aircraft from KWCARIB was also used for transport and reconnaissance tasks following the hurricane. This operation was characterized by a joint deployment of all units and personnel from CZMCARIB and KWCARIB, with additional deployment of units and resources from Defense in the Netherlands. The number of deployed military personnel at the peak was approximately 1000 pax. This military operation was carried out jointly with various Caribbean security partners and lasted until October 31, after which it was scaled down. Military assistance from CZMCARIB provided both soft and hard military support to the authorities of the countries and islands of the Kingdom on several occasions. Some examples include: the Curaçao Militia (CURMIL) was deployed several times in 2017 for crime fighting as part of Ta Basta Awor. In Aruba, 32 RSQN contributed to investigations by the Korps Politie Aruba (KPA) and the Recherche Samenwerkingsteam by providing search capacity. Engineers from CIDW supported the police in Curaçao several times in searching homes and properties as part of judicial investigations. CZMCARIB assisted the authorities in Sint Maarten in searching cells of the penitentiary institution for prohibited substances, mobile phones, and weapons. The Army Company in the West Rotations of the CIDW completed a varied and challenging exercise program. The four rotations were provided by CIDW 23 (C/Berencompagnie 17 Pantserinfanterie-bataljon Garderegiment Prinses Irene), CIDW 24, CIDW 25 from the Alfa-Java infantry company of the 11th Air Mobile Brigade, and CIDW 26 the ‘Stoters’, from the 13th infantry battalion ‘Regiment Stoottroepen Prins Bernhard’ from Assen and is a sister unit of the previous rotation. All CIDW rotations conducted various integrated exercises with CURMIL. The rotations, among other things, monitored several possible landing locations in the context of human trafficking together with CURMIL. Engineers from CIDW 25, together with 32 RSQN, provided support before, during, and after the passage of Hurricane Irma on SXM. Zr.Ms. Pelikaan transported the remaining military personnel of this CIDW rotation to Sint Maarten after this natural disaster, to

sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean also provided emergency assistance there. The rotations frequently supported the local authorities in Curaçao with their engineering capacity during the search for evidence. The Crowd Control Platoon regularly conducted integration training/exercises with the Curaçao Police Corps (KPC) and/or the Curaçao Volunteer Corps (VKC) under the guidance of the Integrated Professional Skills Training of the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee (KMAR). Visiting Units Throughout the year, several units came to Curaçao and Aruba to conduct their training there. CZMCARIB generally supported these exercises. The Defense Relationship Hospitals Institute conducted the final exercise Daktari twice in Curaçao for civilian medical personnel who can be deployed in operational areas. Other visiting Dutch units included snipers and trackers from the Marine Corps, the Defense Diving School, and the Diving and Dismantling Group. The 2nd RECON BN IIMEF USMC conducted maritime (diving) training in August/September in Aruba and Bonaire. Military personnel train for "crowd control."
